---

# Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, circa 1800 (Pre-Statehood)

## Jurisdictional Context

Present-day Alabama did not exist as a political unit around 1800. The region was split across overlapping jurisdictions:

| Jurisdiction | Dates | Area Covered |
|---|---|---|
| **Mississippi Territory** | 1798–1817 | Most of present-day Alabama |
| **Alabama Territory** | 1817–1819 | Eastern portion split off from Mississippi Territory |
| **Spanish West Florida** | until 1813 | Mobile Bay and surrounding coastal lowlands |
| French colonial (background) | 1702–1763 | Mobile area |
| British colonial (background) | 1763–1780 | Mobile area |
| Spanish colonial | 1780–1813 | Mobile District |

> **Critical research rule:** Records created before 1817 are filed under **Mississippi Territory**, not Alabama. County formation was also nascent — Washington County organized in 1800, Madison County in 1808, Baldwin and Monroe counties in 1809. Before those dates, no county-level records exist for most of the region; records are territorial only. The Mobile area runs on a completely separate archival trail through Spanish and French repositories until 1813.

---

## Record Types, Access Levels & Repositories

### 1. Census & Population Schedules

**Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810):** The Mississippi Territory conducted population enumerations in those years covering present-day Alabama settlers. Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *Alabama Genealogy* ("Territorial Records"), these are physically held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH), Montgomery**. They are not separately indexed on FamilySearch for this period.

**Federal census:** The 1800 federal census was conducted under Mississippi Territory; the 1810 census is the first with Alabama coverage. FamilySearch holds:
- **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (collection [2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756)) — 287,634 records — **index only, no images attached**
- **"Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890"** (collection [1927171](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171)) — 198,340 records — **index only, no images attached**

For the 1800 federal census, search under Mississippi Territory at NARA or Ancestry.

---

### 2. Land Records ⭐ *(richest source for this period)*

Alabama is a **federal land state** — original titles came from the General Land Office, not the state. This makes federal-level land records essential.

- **Bureau of Land Management General Land Office (GLO)** — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov): Federal land patents from the early 1800s onward. Free online access with images. Begin here for any ancestor who received a first-title patent.
- **"Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907"** (collection [1919694](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694)) — 312,450 indexed records, 156,225 images. This collection begins at the territorial era (1798) and directly covers land transactions in what is now Alabama before it separated from Mississippi Territory. **Indexed + images. Search this collection for all pre-1817 Alabama land activity.**
- **Spanish land grants (Mobile District, pre-1813):** Original grants are at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain**. Copies are at the **Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.**
- **ADAH, Montgomery:** Holds territorial-era land grant records, tax digests, and related documents for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory.

---

### 3. Tax Records *(census substitutes)*

Territorial-era tax lists and tax digests survive and name heads of household for years between formal censuses — one of the best substitutes for the absent early census years. Per the FamilySearch Wiki (*Alabama Genealogy*, "Territorial Records"), these are among the records held at **ADAH, Montgomery**. No separately name-indexed FamilySearch collection for territorial-era Alabama tax lists was returned — check the **ADAH catalog** directly for microfilm availability.

---

### 4. Church Records

Civil registration (birth/marriage/death certificates) did not exist in this period. Church records are the **only source** for vital events.

- **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (collection [1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396)) — 156,789 records, 78,394 images. **Indexed + images.** Earliest entries (1803–1819) cover the territorial period, primarily Baptist and Methodist congregations that followed American settlement into the region.
- **"Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950"** (collection [2034891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891)) — 87,654 records, 43,827 images. **Indexed + images.** May include territorial-era communities in what is now Alabama.
- **Catholic records, Mobile area:** The Mobile parish dates to the French colonial era. Spanish-era Catholic registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are held at the **Archivo General de Indias, Seville**, and in microfilm at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. French colonial registers are at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France**, with microfilm copies at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. ⚠️ These are in French and Spanish — researcher must read those languages or engage a translator.

---

### 5. Marriage Records

- **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (collection [1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408)) — 612,345 indexed records, 306,172 images. **Indexed + images.** County-level marriage bonds and licenses begin only with county formation (~1809). **Before 1809, no county marriage records exist** — church registers are the sole surviving source.

---

### 6. Probate Records

- **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (collection [1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764)) — 438,210 indexed records, 219,105 images. **Indexed + images.** County-level probate begins with county formation (1809+).
- For deaths and estates in the territorial era (pre-1809), consult territorial court records at ADAH and search the Mississippi Territory court collection below.

---

### 7. Court Records

- **"Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920"** (collection [1855293](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293)) — 245,670 indexed records, 122,835 images. **Indexed + images.** Territorial-era court records covering what is now both Mississippi and Alabama, starting 1799.
- **ADAH, Montgomery:** Holds territorial-era court records for the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory, including militia rolls (FamilySearch Wiki, *Alabama Genealogy*, "Territorial Records").

---

### 8. Military Records

- **NARA, Washington, D.C. & NARA Southeast Region (Morrow, GA):** Service records, pension files, and bounty-land warrant applications for territorial militia and U.S. Army service.
- **Fold3** (fold3.com): Digitized War of 1812 service records and pension files; useful for the Creek War period (1813–1814), which generated significant militia records for men in present-day Alabama.
- **ADAH, Montgomery:** State adjutant general records and territorial-era militia rolls.

---

### 9. Colonial Records — Mobile Area (Spanish & French)

For ancestors in the **Mobile Bay area before 1813**, the research trail runs through European archives:

| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain** | Original Spanish census returns, church registers, land grants for Mobile District (1780–1813); largely physical |
| **Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.** | Copies of Spanish colonial records |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France** | Original French colonial records (1702–1763) |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL** | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial records — most accessible local access point |

Per the FamilySearch Wiki (*Alabama Genealogy*, "Colonial Records"), Spanish records of the Mobile District include census returns, church registers, and land grants; French records are similarly documented in those archives.

---

### 10. Newspapers

Territorial-era Alabama newspapers are sparse before 1811. The **Library of Congress Chronicling America** project ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) provides free access. **Newspapers.com** also holds historical Alabama papers, though coverage before statehood is limited.

---

## Master Repository Table

| Repository | What It Holds for circa 1800 | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH), Montgomery, AL** | Territorial censuses (1801–1810), land grants, tax lists, militia rolls, court records | In person; ADAH online catalog at archives.alabama.gov |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Alabama and Mississippi Territory indexed collections — marriages, probate, church, land, court | Free online; some images browse-only |
| **BLM General Land Office** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Federal land patents from early 1800s | Free online with images |
| **NARA, Washington D.C. & Atlanta** | Military service, pension files, federal land records | In person or through Fold3/Ancestry |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives, Mobile, AL** | Microfilm of French and Spanish colonial registers | In person |
| **Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain** | Original Spanish colonial records, Mobile District | In person or correspondence; some digitized via PARES portal |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence** | Original French colonial records | In person |
| **Library of Congress, Washington, D.C.** | Copies of Spanish colonial records | In person; some digitized |

---

## Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Level |
|---|---|
| County marriages, 1809+ | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Probate records, 1809+ | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Church records, 1803+ | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Territorial/state land records, 1798+ (MS scope) | ✅ Indexed + images |
| County court records, 1799+ (MS scope) | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Census substitutes, Alabama 1810+ | ⚠️ Index only — no images |
| Census substitutes, Mississippi 1792+ | ⚠️ Index only — no images |
| Territorial censuses 1801–1810 | 🔴 Physical only at ADAH |
| Spanish/French colonial records | 🔴 Physical/microfilm; overseas archives and Mobile Municipal Archives |
| Territorial-era tax lists | 🔴 Physical at ADAH — check ADAH catalog |

---

## Top Research Warnings

1. **Search Mississippi Territory collections, not just Alabama.** All FamilySearch collections covering the 1798–1817 period are filed under "Mississippi." If you only search Alabama, you will miss the earliest digitized territorial records.
2. **County structure was absent or just forming.** Most of present-day Alabama had no county government before 1808–1809. Records before that are territorial-level or simply don't exist yet.
3. **Mobile is a different research world.** Southern Alabama (Mobile, Baldwin area) was under Spanish West Florida until 1813 — these records are in Spanish, held overseas, and require the Archivo General de Indias trail, not the American territorial trail.
4. **No civil vital registration** existed. Church records and county marriage bonds (post-1809) are the only surviving sources for births, marriages, and deaths.
5. **The FamilySearch Alabama census substitute collection (1810–1890) carries no images** — after finding a hit in the index, you must obtain the original at ADAH or through a microfilm request.

## Locality Research Guide: Arkansas Region, Pre-1800 (Spanish Colonial Period)

---

### Jurisdictional History

The Arkansas region had three successive colonial authorities before it became U.S. territory — each created a distinct record trail:

| Period | Authority | Administrative center |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1763 | French La Louisiane | Arkansas Post (established 1686) |
| 1763–1800 | Spanish colonial (Treaty of Paris) | Arkansas Post |
| 1800 | French (Treaty of San Ildefonso, secret) | — |
| 1803 | United States (Louisiana Purchase) | — |
| 1819 | Arkansas Territory | — |
| 1836+ | State of Arkansas | — |

**Critical research fact:** Before 1836, the modern state of Arkansas did not exist as a named jurisdiction. Virtually the entire European-contact population of the region was concentrated at a single post: **Arkansas Post** (present-day Arkansas County). Any record from this period will almost certainly be filed under Arkansas Post, the District of Arkansas, or the Province of Louisiana — not "Arkansas." Searching FamilySearch or any repository under the state name alone will miss these records.

*(Source: Wikipedia article "Arkansas"; FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records")*

---

### Record Types, Repositories & Access

#### 1. Sacramental Registers (Catholic Church)
**Dates:** Early 1700s–1800 (French-era registrations begin c. 1700; Spanish-era run 1763–1800)

French Catholic missionaries maintained baptismal, marriage, and burial registers at Arkansas Post from the early eighteenth century. These record European settlers and Native Americans alike and are the richest personal-name source surviving from the colonial period.

**FamilySearch digitized volume — the only pre-1800 Arkansas record available online:**

| Detail | Value |
|---|---|
| Image Group Number | 008814402 |
| Images | 64 |
| Coverage | Arkansas Post, 1763–1800 |
| Record type | Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) |
| Indexed? | **No** — 0% name-searchable |
| Full-text searchable? | **No** |
| Language | **Spanish** |
| Access | **Browse-only, image by image** |

⚠️ **This volume must be browsed page-by-page with no search capability. The register is in Spanish — researchers must be able to read colonial Spanish ecclesiastical script or engage a translator.**

Physical/microfilm originals and transcriptions are also held at:
- **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** — original registers
- **Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock** — transcribed copies

*(Source: FamilySearch volume search; FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy — Church Records")*

---

#### 2. Spanish Colonial Civil & Military Records (Padrones, Land Concessions, Post Records)
**Dates:** 1763–1800

Under Spanish administration, the commandant at Arkansas Post generated:
- **Padrones** (census lists): periodic household enumerations giving names, ages, and relationships
- **Land concessions**: grants naming grantees and describing tracts
- **Military post records**: muster rolls and correspondence naming soldiers and their families

**⚠️ None of these record classes appear in FamilySearch's indexed collections** — `collections_search` returned zero collections covering the pre-1800 Arkansas period. These records survive primarily in physical or microfilm form at:

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, 1 Capitol Mall, Little Rock, AR | Microfilm and transcriptions of colonial records; state archives | In-person or by mail; some finding aids online |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Original Spanish colonial administrative records for Louisiana, including Arkansas Post | In-person or through a professional researcher in Spain; some digitization via Portal de Archivos Españoles (PARES) |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington DC | Microfilm copies of selected Spanish colonial Louisiana records | Reading room access; some online via the Library's digital collections |

*(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records")*

---

#### 3. French Colonial Records (Pre-1763)
**Dates:** 1686–1763

Records from the French La Louisiane era are held primarily in French archives and Louisiana repositories rather than in Arkansas collections. These include correspondence, concessions, and any sacramental registers kept before Spanish takeover.

- **Archives nationales d'outre-mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France — original French colonial Louisiana records; searchable finding aids online at [anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)
- **Louisiana State Archives / Louisiana Historical Center**, New Orleans — transcripts and microfilm of French Louisiana records affecting the Arkansas region
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives** — some French-era land and legal transactions

---

#### 4. FamilySearch Indexed Collections (Post-1800 — Context Only)
The three FamilySearch indexed collections for Arkansas all **postdate the target period** and are not primary sources for pre-1800 research, but may help bridge into the territorial era if a family survived into the 1820s–1870s:

| Collection | Date Range | Records |
|---|---|---|
| Arkansas, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1819–1870 | 1819–1870 | 178,345 indexed |
| Arkansas, County Marriages, 1837–1957 | 1837–1957 | 389,210 indexed |
| Arkansas, Freedmen's Bureau Field Office Records, 1865–1872 | 1865–1872 | 45,678 indexed |

---

#### 5. External Repositories (Curated Links)
FamilySearch's curated external links for Arkansas in the 1686–1800 window returned only generic national repositories (NARA, Fold3, Ancestry census collection, FindAGrave, Newspapers.com). **None of these hold meaningful pre-1800 Arkansas-specific records.** For this period, bypass these and go directly to the repositories in sections 2–3 above.

---

### Coverage Summary & Digitization Gaps

| Record class | Online & indexed | Online browse-only | Physical/microfilm only |
|---|---|---|---|
| Spanish-era sacramental registers (Arkansas Post, 1763–1800) | — | ✅ FamilySearch vol. 008814402 (64 images, Spanish) | Diocese of Little Rock; AHC |
| Spanish padrones & land concessions | — | — | ✅ AHC; AGI Seville; Library of Congress |
| French-era church & civil records (pre-1763) | — | — | ✅ ANOM Aix-en-Provence; Louisiana Historical Center |
| Military post records (both eras) | — | — | ✅ AGI Seville; NARA (post-1803 only) |

**Bottom line on digitization:** Only one digitized pre-1800 volume exists on FamilySearch for this region — 64 browse-only images of Spanish sacramental registers in Spanish. Everything else requires contacting physical repositories or archives in Arkansas, Louisiana, or Spain.

---

### Key Research Quirks & Warnings

1. **Search "Arkansas Post," not "Arkansas."** No jurisdiction called "Arkansas" existed before 1819. Colonial-era records use Arkansas Post, Poste des Arkansas, Puesto de los Arkancas, or District of Arkansas.
2. **Spanish records are in Spanish; French records in French.** Colonial handwriting — particularly colonial Spanish ecclesiastical cursive — requires specialized paleographic skill or a professional transcriber.
3. **The single FamilySearch volume (008814402) is the starting point online,** but it covers only 1763–1800 sacramental records at one post. If your ancestor appears nowhere in those 64 images, the next step is a direct inquiry to the Arkansas History Commission.
4. **Trace the family through the Louisiana Purchase transition.** If your ancestor was alive in 1803, they may appear in early American-era records (territorial land claims, 1810 or 1820 census) that bridge back to colonial identity. The Arkansas Compiled Census Substitutes collection (1819–1870) is worth checking for continuity.
5. **Spanish land claims were adjudicated after 1803.** The U.S. Board of Land Commissioners reviewed Spanish and French land grants after the Louisiana Purchase. These claim files, held at NARA and partially indexed, sometimes contain detailed family testimony from pre-1800 settlers — a valuable substitute source when church registers are silent.

---

### Where to Start

1. **Browse FamilySearch image group 008814402** (Arkansas Post sacramental registers, 1763–1800) — free, 64 images, no index so plan to look at every page.
2. **Contact the Arkansas History Commission** (arkansasheritage.com) — best single repository for colonial Arkansas transcriptions and microfilm.
3. **Search PARES** ([pares.mcu.es](https://pares.mcu.es)) — Spain's online portal to the Archivo General de Indias, which holds the original administrative records of Spanish Louisiana including Arkansas Post.
4. **Check ANOM** for French-era records predating 1763.
5. **Review U.S. Board of Land Commissioners claim files at NARA** if the family held land — these post-1803 files frequently document colonial-era residence.

# 📍 Locality Research Guide
## Ohio (pre-statehood) · Northwest Territory · circa 1790

---

## 1. Jurisdictional History & Boundary Changes

This period requires understanding **two overlapping jurisdictional layers** — the territorial government and its rapidly proliferating counties — because records were created at both levels and are now held in separate repositories.

| Period | Governing Jurisdiction | What This Means for Records |
|---|---|---|
| 1787–1788 | **Northwest Territory** (no organized counties yet) | Virtually no civil records; federal land survey begins (Seven Ranges, 1785+) |
| 1788–1790 | **Washington County, N.W. Territory** | First organized county; covers all of present-day Ohio east of the Scioto River |
| 1790–1803 | Washington County + **Hamilton County** (formed 1790) | Southwest Ohio splits off; records bifurcate between the two |
| 1803 | **Ohio** achieves statehood (March 1) | State-level record-keeping begins; earlier county records remain at county level |

> ⚠️ **Critical researcher note:** For any event in Ohio before 1803, determine *which county held jurisdiction at the time and place of the event* — and look for records there, not under "Ohio" statehood collections. Washington County records (at the Ohio History Connection and Marietta College) are the primary pre-statehood archive for most of the territory. A record filed under Washington County, Northwest Territory and one filed under Washington County, Ohio are part of one continuous research trail — search both.

### Special Land Districts (affect all land research)

Three distinct land-grant systems operated in what became Ohio, each with separate record repositories:

| District | Location | Survey System | Primary Records Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between Scioto and Little Miami Rivers | Metes-and-bounds | Virginia State Library / Library of Virginia |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Township grid | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **Ohio Company Purchase / Seven Ranges** | Southeastern Ohio (Marietta area) | Federal rectangular survey | BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) |

---

## 2. Population Context

No population data was returned by the tool for this fixture. Historically, Ohio's non-Indigenous population was extremely small in 1790 — concentrated around Marietta (Ohio Company settlers, arriving 1788) and the Cincinnati area (Fort Washington, 1789). Most of the territory was unsurveyed and unorganized. This sparse settlement directly explains the thin documentary record.

---

## 3. Available Records

### 🔴 Federal Census — **Gap for 1790; coverage begins 1800**

The **1790 federal census did not enumerate the Northwest Territory**. Ohio's earliest federal census is **1800**, by which time statehood was imminent. There is no substitute enumeration for 1790 Ohio.

> **Substitute strategy:** Use territorial tax lists (see below) and land entry records as census substitutes for 1790.

---

### 🟡 Land Records — **Primary source for this period**

Land records are the single most important genealogical source for pre-statehood Ohio — they are often the only proof that a person was present in the territory.

**FamilySearch collection (indexed):**
- **Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840** (Collection ID: 1542187) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Starts at statehood/territorial founding. Directly overlaps target period. Access at: [familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187)

**Digitized volumes (browse-only):**
- **Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799** (Image Group 005112233) — 51 images; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** → must be browsed image by image. These are the closest to pure 1790 land documentation FamilySearch holds in digitized form.

**Physical/external repositories:**
- **BLM General Land Office** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) — federal land patent database; searchable by name for Ohio Company Purchase and Seven Ranges patents
- **Virginia State Library / Library of Virginia** — Virginia Military District warrants; free online database at lva.virginia.gov
- **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland) — Connecticut Western Reserve land records

---

### 🟡 Tax Records — **Best 1790-era census substitute**

Territorial and early county tax lists name heads of household, making them functional census substitutes when no enumeration exists.

**FamilySearch collection (indexed):**
- **Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850** (Collection ID: 1987542) — 345,890 records. Begins at 1800; covers early statehood but **not the 1790 territorial period**.

**Digitized volume (partially accessible):**
- **Washington County Tax Records, 1799–1803** (Image Group 005112240) — 73 images; **12% name-indexed**, not full-text searchable. Most records require browsing. Covers the last years of territorial Ohio — the nearest available tax documentation to 1790 in FamilySearch's digitized holdings.

> **Gap note:** Tax records from 1788–1799 for Washington and Hamilton Counties appear not to be digitized or indexed on FamilySearch. Consult the **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) for manuscript tax lists from this period.

---

### 🟢 Marriage Records — **Indexed, good early coverage**

- **Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013** (Collection ID: 1803785) — 1,523,678 records, 761,839 images. Starts **1789** — the earliest indexed civil record collection for Ohio on FamilySearch. Directly covers the target window. Access: [familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785)

> Search this collection first for any marriage event from 1789 onward. Records are organized by county — remember that pre-1790 events fall under Washington County, and post-1790 southwestern Ohio events under Hamilton County.

---

### 🟢 Church Records — **Earliest documentary source**

- **Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950** (Collection ID: 2246917) — 678,234 records, 339,117 images. Starts **1787** — the earliest FamilySearch collection covering Ohio at all. Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) predate all civil registration and are crucial for the 1787–1803 window. Access: [familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917)

> The Ohio Company brought Congregationalist settlers to Marietta in 1788; Presbyterian and Methodist circuits followed in the early 1790s. Church records from Marietta (Washington County) are especially important for the earliest Ohio settlers.

---

### 🔵 Military Records — **Vital for identifying early settlers**

Many of Ohio's earliest non-Indigenous settlers were **Revolutionary War veterans** who received land bounty warrants in the Virginia Military District or purchased Ohio Company tracts. Military records thus double as migration evidence.

- **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://fold3.com)) — Revolutionary War service records and pension files (NARA originals)
- **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://archives.gov)) — Revolutionary War pension files (Series M804); bounty land warrant applications; many are fully digitized and searchable by name
- **Ancestry.com** — U.S. Federal Census collection (1800 onward for Ohio)

---

### 🔴 Death Records — **Not available for this period**

- **Ohio, County Death Records, 1840–2001** (Collection ID: 1417891) — starts 1840; **entirely outside the 1790 target window**. No civil death registration existed in territorial Ohio.

> **Substitute:** Church burial registers (in the Church Records collection above), cemetery inscriptions (FindAGrave at [findagrave.com](https://findagrave.com)), and estate/probate records are the only death documentation for 1790.

---

### 🔵 Probate & Court Records

Court and probate records from Washington County (1788–) and Hamilton County (1790–) are held physically at:
- **Ohio History Connection**, 800 E. 17th Ave., Columbus, OH — state archives, holds territorial-era records
- **Washington County Probate Court**, Marietta, OH — original county records
- **Hamilton County Probate Court**, Cincinnati, OH

FamilySearch has not returned digitized probate volumes for the 1775–1810 window in this survey — treat these as **physical-only** until confirmed otherwise.

---

### 🔵 Newspapers

- **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://newspapers.com)) — Historical newspapers. The *Centinel of the North-Western Territory* (Cincinnati, 1793) is the first newspaper in the territory; very sparse coverage for 1790 specifically.

---

## 4. Access Summary by Record Type

| Record Type | FamilySearch Collection | Date Coverage | Access Level | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Land Records | 1542187 | 1787–1840 | Indexed + images | Best pre-statehood source |
| Territorial Land Records (volumes) | Image Group 005112233 | 1788–1799 | **Browse-only** (0% indexed) | Must browse image by image |
| Church Records | 2246917 | 1787–1950 | Indexed + images | Earliest FamilySearch Ohio collection |
| Marriages | 1803785 | 1789–2013 | Indexed + images | Starts 1789; by county |
| Tax Records (early county) | Image Group 005112240 | 1799–1803 | 12% indexed, rest browse-only | Near-1790 substitute; mostly browse |
| Tax Records (state) | 1987542 | 1800–1850 | Indexed + images | Starts after target period |
| Death Records | 1417891 | 1840–2001 | Indexed + images | **Outside target window** |
| Federal Census | — | 1800+ | — | **No 1790 census for Ohio** |
| Military/Pension | NARA / Fold3 | 1775–1800 | Name-searchable online | Key for settler identification |
| Probate/Court | Physical only | 1788+ | Physical repositories | Ohio History Connection; county courts |

---

## 5. Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection** (Columbus) | State archives; territorial-era records; tax lists; early court records | ohiohistory.org |
| **Washington County Probate Court** (Marietta) | Original county records from 1788 | On-site |
| **Hamilton County Probate Court** (Cincinnati) | County records from 1790 | On-site |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents | glorecords.blm.gov (free, online) |
| **Library of Virginia** | Virginia Military District warrants | lva.virginia.gov (online) |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society** (Cleveland) | Connecticut Western Reserve land records | wrhs.org |
| **NARA** | Rev. War pensions; military records | archives.gov |
| **FamilySearch** | Digitized collections listed above | familysearch.org |

---

## 6. Research Strategy Recommendations

1. **Start with land records**, not vital records — the Land Records (1787–1840) and BLM GLO databases are the most likely sources to place a person in the territory in 1790.
2. **Identify the correct county at the time of the event.** Before 1790, everything is Washington County. After 1790, check whether the location falls in the southwest (Hamilton County) or elsewhere (still Washington).
3. **Use the 1800 federal census as a near-substitute** for 1790 — it will show household members and neighbors, many of whom were already present in 1790.
4. **Check which land district applies** before searching land records — Virginia Military District, Connecticut Western Reserve, and Seven Ranges/Ohio Company records are held in entirely different repositories with different indexing.
5. **Revolutionary War pension files (NARA M804)** are crucial: many early Ohio settlers filed pension claims describing when and where they settled, naming family members and witnesses.
6. **Church records (1787+)** are the only pre-statehood vital-event documentation; the Marietta Congregationalist and Cincinnati-area Methodist/Presbyterian registers are the most likely to survive.
7. **Browse the Northwest Territory Territorial Land Records volume** (Image Group 005112233, 51 images) image by image — it is 0% indexed but covers 1788–1799 directly.

---

The wiki_place_page tool returned generic content rather than an Ohio-specific page — consult the [FamilySearch Ohio Genealogy wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy) directly for additional detail.*

The documentary record is thin but navigable: land, church, and military records are your best allies, and the Ohio History Connection in Columbus is the single most important physical repository for this period.

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California admitted to statehood **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely — there is no American territorial phase for records purposes. U.S. military/civilian governance bridged the 1848–1850 gap after the Mexican-American War.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco (commercial hub)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Alta California (Mexico) until 1848; United States thereafter
- **Population during period:** Approximately **300,000 migrants** arrived during the Gold Rush (1848–1855), drawn from across the United States and internationally (Wikipedia, "California Gold Rush")
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominant 1848–1855; diversifying into agriculture, commerce, and trade thereafter
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — migrants from all U.S. states, Mexico, Chile, China, Australia, and Europe (Wikipedia: "diverse origins")
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood September 9, 1850; state census conducted 1852

## Boundary changes
- California's **27 original counties** were created by the first state legislature in 1850; many have since been subdivided. Records before a county's formation date are held by the parent county.
- Key Gold Rush mining counties: **El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, and Sacramento**
- Before 1848: records fall under Mexican Alta California (mission and land-grant records) — outside the Gold Rush window but relevant for families with deeper California roots
- California bypassed territorial status, so 1850 county records are the earliest American administrative records

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level recording began **1850** with statehood; **no statewide civil registration** existed during this period
- **Births:** FamilySearch collection 2017276 — *California, County Births, 1850–1919* — 789,456 records / ~395K images — **Indexed + images** (free, FamilySearch)
- **Marriages:** FamilySearch collection 1452832 — *California, County Marriages, 1850–1952* — 567,890 records / ~284K images — **Indexed + images** (free, FamilySearch)
- **Deaths:** No dedicated county death collection appeared in FamilySearch collections_search results for this period — treat as a **coverage gap**; check county courthouses and California State Archives directly
- **Gaps:** Early compliance was inconsistent. The transient miner population meant many deaths, births, and marriages went entirely unrecorded in county registers

### Church records
- **Mission records (Spanish/Mexican era):** FamilySearch collection 1804372 — *California, Mission Records, 1769–1850* — 98,765 records / ~49K images — **Indexed + images**. Covers the Catholic Franciscan mission system; most relevant for families predating the Gold Rush. These records are in Spanish and Latin.
- **Post-1850 denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, and Congregationalist congregations arrived with the Gold Rush wave; Catholic parish records continued post-mission
- **Where held:** Mission records on FamilySearch; post-1850 parish records at diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco, Diocese of Monterey) and FamilySearch microfilm — extent of digitization for 1850s registers is unclear from tool results

### Census records
- **1850 federal census** ⚠️ — **Partially destroyed**: some California county returns are missing (FamilySearch wiki, "California Genealogy — Pre-Statehood Records"). Do not assume absence = not in California; cross-check with the 1852 state census. Surviving returns are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **1852 California state census** ⭐ — FamilySearch volume 006601001 — 522 images — **88% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — the single most important Gold Rush census source, filling the gap between the damaged 1850 and the complete 1860 federal census. Captures the peak Gold Rush population.
- **1860 federal census** — Complete for California; indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Mortality schedules** — 1850 and 1860 mortality schedules record deaths in the year preceding the census; available on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Mining claim records
- **FamilySearch volume 006601002** — Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855 — 340 images — ⚠️ **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.** Must be worked image by image with no search capability.
- **County-level records:** Mining claim records were filed at **county recorders' offices** (FamilySearch wiki, "California Genealogy — Gold Rush Records"). El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, and Calaveras are the primary counties.
- **Where held:** County recorders' offices (originals); California State Archives; some volumes on FamilySearch (browse-only)

### Immigration and arrival records
- **Ship passenger manifests:** Arrivals by sea at San Francisco are documented in passenger lists held at the **National Archives, Pacific Region, San Bruno, California** — not Washington D.C. (FamilySearch wiki, "California Genealogy — Gold Rush Records"). Cross-reference with Ancestry and FamilySearch passenger-list collections.
- **Port arrival registers (Sacramento):** FamilySearch volume 006601003 — Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858 — 298 images — ⚠️ **Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable.**
- **Overland migrants:** No single centralized record. Consult overland trail diaries, journals, and manuscript collections at the Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and California State Library.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists record every person aboard, including children. Examine the full manifest when researching a family.

### Land records
- **System:** Federal land state — patents issued by the U.S. Bureau of Land Management. The **BLM General Land Office website** (glorecords.blm.gov) has federal land patents searchable by name, free online.
- **Spanish/Mexican land grants:** Pre-statehood ranchos were adjudicated by the U.S. Land Commission after 1851; adjudication records at NARA and California State Archives
- **County deed records:** Property transfers recorded at county recorders' offices from 1850
- **Access:** BLM GLO (free, online); county recorders (physical/mail); California State Archives (in-person or catalog)

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, inventories, guardianships — filed at county level from 1850
- **Naturalization:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — California county superior courts, U.S. Circuit Court, U.S. District Court. NARA San Bruno holds federal court records.
- **Access:** Mostly **physical only** for this period — county courthouses and California State Archives. Not widely digitized.

### Military records
- **Mexican-American War (1846–1848):** Immediately precedes Gold Rush; service records and pension files at NARA
- **Civil War (1861–1865):** California Volunteer units served in the West; many Gold Rush-era men later enlisted. Records at NARA and Fold3 (subscription).
- **California State Militia:** Records at California State Archives
- **Access:** Fold3 (subscription); NARA (free with appointment or written request)

### Voter registration — Great Registers ⭐
- **FamilySearch collection 1923340** — *California, Great Registers, 1866–1910* — 1,345,678 records — **Indexed + images** ⚠️ Begins **1866**, just outside the strict window, but the earliest volumes capture men who arrived during the Gold Rush and settled permanently. Contains name, age, **birthplace**, occupation, and physical description — unusually rich detail for identifying origins.

### Cemetery records
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) has California transcriptions; coverage varies widely by county
- **Gaps:** Many Gold Rush mining camps had informal or unmarked burials with no surviving sexton records

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849–1891), *Sacramento Daily Union* (1851–), and numerous mining district papers — rich for obituaries, legal notices, mining news, and land sales
- **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (cdnc.ucr.edu) — **free, full-text searchable** — an often-overlooked high-value source
- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) — broader aggregated coverage

### Occupational and organizational records
- **Mining district records:** Self-governing mining districts maintained claim registers, bylaws, and meeting minutes — held at county recorders' offices or local historical societies; not digitized
- **Fraternal organizations:** Odd Fellows, Masons active from early 1850s; membership records at state/local lodge archives
- **City directories:** San Francisco and Sacramento had early city directories from the 1850s — useful for locating individuals by address and occupation

# Locality Guide: California, United States (1848–1865)

## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** California admitted to statehood **September 9, 1850**, bypassing territorial status entirely — there is no American territorial phase for records purposes. U.S. military/civilian governance bridged the 1848–1850 gap after the Mexican-American War.
- **County seat / administrative center:** Sacramento (state capital); San Francisco (commercial hub)
- **Parent jurisdiction:** Alta California (Mexico) until 1848; United States thereafter
- **Population during period:** Approximately **300,000 migrants** arrived during the Gold Rush (1848–1855), drawn from across the United States and internationally (Wikipedia, "California Gold Rush")
- **Economy:** Gold mining dominant 1848–1855; diversifying into agriculture, commerce, and trade thereafter
- **Ethnic composition:** Highly diverse — migrants from all U.S. states, Mexico, Chile, China, Australia, and Europe
- **Key historical events:** Gold discovered at Sutter's Mill, January 24, 1848; California statehood September 9, 1850; state census conducted 1852

## Boundary changes
- California's **27 original counties** were created by the first state legislature in 1850; many have since been subdivided. Records before a county's formation date are held by the parent county.
- Key Gold Rush mining counties: **El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, and Sacramento**
- Before 1848: records fall under Mexican Alta California (mission and land-grant records)
- California bypassed territorial status, so 1850 county records are the earliest American administrative records

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** County-level recording began **1850**; **no statewide civil registration** existed during this period
- **Births:** FamilySearch collection 2017276 — *California, County Births, 1850–1919* — 789,456 records / ~395K images — **Indexed + images** (free)
- **Marriages:** FamilySearch collection 1452832 — *California, County Marriages, 1850–1952* — 567,890 records / ~284K images — **Indexed + images** (free)
- **Deaths:** No dedicated county death collection found in FamilySearch for this period — **coverage gap**; check county courthouses and California State Archives directly
- **Gaps:** Transient miner population meant many deaths, births, and marriages went unrecorded

### Church records
- **Mission records:** FamilySearch collection 1804372 — *California, Mission Records, 1769–1850* — 98,765 records / ~49K images — **Indexed + images**. Spanish/Latin; covers pre-Gold Rush Catholic mission system.
- **Post-1850 denominations:** Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Congregationalist arrived with the Gold Rush; Catholic parishes continued
- **Where held:** Mission records on FamilySearch; post-1850 parish records at diocesan archives (Archdiocese of San Francisco, Diocese of Monterey) and FamilySearch microfilm

### Census records
- **1850 federal census** ⚠️ — **Partially destroyed**: some county returns are missing (FamilySearch wiki, "California Genealogy"). Surviving returns indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **1852 California state census** ⭐ — FamilySearch volume 006601001 — 522 images — **88% name-indexed, full-text searchable** — the single most important Gold Rush census source
- **1860 federal census** — Complete for California; indexed + images on Ancestry and FamilySearch
- **Mortality schedules** — 1850 and 1860 schedules record deaths in the preceding year; on Ancestry and FamilySearch

### Mining claim records
- **FamilySearch volume 006601002** — Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco, 1849–1855 — 340 images — ⚠️ **Browse-only: 0% indexed, not full-text searchable**
- **County-level records:** Filed at county recorders' offices (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras). Not digitized.

### Immigration and arrival records
- **Ship passenger manifests:** Held at **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** (not Washington D.C.). Cross-reference Ancestry and FamilySearch passenger-list collections.
- **Port arrival registers (Sacramento):** FamilySearch volume 006601003 — 298 images — ⚠️ **Browse-only: 0% indexed, not full-text searchable**
- **Overland migrants:** No centralized record; consult manuscript collections at Bancroft Library (UC Berkeley) and California State Library

### Land records
- **System:** Federal land state — BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) has federal patents searchable by name, free online
- **Spanish/Mexican land grants:** Adjudicated post-1851 by U.S. Land Commission; records at NARA and California State Archives
- **County deed records:** At county recorders' offices from 1850

### Probate and court records
- Filed at county level from 1850; mostly **physical only** — county courthouses and California State Archives
- Pre-1906 naturalizations in any court of record; NARA San Bruno holds federal court records

### Military records
- Mexican-American War (1846–1848): service records and pension files at NARA
- Civil War (1861–1865): California Volunteer units; records at NARA and Fold3 (subscription)
- California State Militia records at California State Archives

### Voter registration — Great Registers ⭐
- FamilySearch collection 1923340 — *California, Great Registers, 1866–1910* — 1,345,678 records — **Indexed + images** ⚠️ Begins 1866 but captures Gold Rush settlers; includes birthplace, age, occupation, and physical description

### Cemetery records
- FindAGrave (findagrave.com) — free; coverage varies by county
- Many mining camp burials were informal with no surviving sexton records

### Newspaper records
- *Alta California* (San Francisco, 1849–1891), *Sacramento Daily Union* (1851–), and mining district papers
- **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (cdnc.ucr.edu) — **free, full-text searchable**
- Newspapers.com — subscription

### Occupational and organizational records
- Mining district records: claim registers, bylaws, meeting minutes — at county recorders' offices or local historical societies; not digitized
- Fraternal organizations (Odd Fellows, Masons) active from early 1850s; records at lodge archives
- City directories for San Francisco and Sacramento from the 1850s

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | County Births 1850–1919 (789K records); County Marriages 1850–1952 (568K records); Mission Records 1769–1850 (99K records); Great Registers 1866–1910 (1.35M records); State Census 1850–1852 (522 images, 88% indexed); Mining Claim Registers 1849–1855 (340 images, browse-only); Port Arrival Registers 1849–1858 (298 images, browse-only) | Free |
| Ancestry | U.S. Federal Census 1850, 1860; passenger lists; mortality schedules | Subscription |
| FindAGrave | Cemetery records | Free |

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| National Archives, Pacific Region — San Bruno, CA | Ship passenger manifests, federal court naturalizations, federal land records | In-person / written request |
| California State Archives — Sacramento | State census, land grant adjudications, militia records | In-person / online catalog |
| California State Library — Sacramento | Manuscripts, newspapers, Gold Rush diaries | In-person |
| Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley | Gold Rush manuscripts, overland diaries, photographs | In-person (appointment) |
| County courthouses | Deed books, probate files, marriage originals | In-person / mail |

- County-level death records for most of this period

- Probate case files for most Gold Rush-era counties
- Mining district bylaws and meeting minutes
- Fraternal organization membership records
- Overland trail documentation (at Bancroft Library and California State Library)

6. **County is the key jurisdictional unit** — identify the specific county before searching vital, land, probate, and court records

8. **Overland migrants leave a different paper trail than sea arrivals** — Bancroft Library and California State Library manuscript collections are the best sources

# Locality Guide: New York City, Colonial Period (1700–1783)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Founded:** Dutch colony New Amsterdam, 1626; seized by England in 1664 and renamed New York City
- **Colonial authority:** New York Province (British royal colony) throughout the 1700s; the city served as its capital
- **Administrative structure:** Governed through elected wards within the city; a Mayor's Court held civil and criminal jurisdiction (*per FamilySearch Wiki: New York City Genealogy*)
- **Economy:** Major commercial seaport; trade, mercantile, and maritime occupations dominated
- **Religious denominations present:** Dutch Reformed (congregation dating to 1639), Anglican/Church of England (Trinity Church), and Presbyterian churches all kept extensive records (*Wikipedia; FamilySearch Wiki*)
- **Population:** No population figures were returned for this period by the place population tool; colonial NYC grew substantially through the 1700s but no census-based counts are available here
- **Key events:** British occupation and commercial growth through the Seven Years' War (1754–63); American Revolution and British military occupation of the city (1776–1783)

---

## Boundary and jurisdictional changes

- New York City's boundaries in the 1700s were confined to the southern tip of Manhattan Island. The surrounding counties (Kings, Queens, Richmond, Westchester) were separate jurisdictions — records for residents outside Manhattan proper were created in those counties, not New York County.
- **1700–1776:** City governed as part of New York Province under British colonial authority. Colonial records are held by the New York State Archives (New York Colonial Manuscripts series) and in county/city-level repositories.
- **1776–1783:** British military occupation during the Revolutionary War. Administrative disruption affected record-keeping during this window.
- **Post-1788:** New York becomes a U.S. state (dateRange +1788 per place_search). State-level record series begin.

> **Researcher note:** Records created during the colonial period follow the jurisdiction that created them — the colonial provincial government, the Mayor's Court, and individual churches — not modern city agencies. Do not assume modern online databases hold these records.

---

## Available record types

### Church records — **PRIMARY SOURCE for this period**
Civil registration did not exist in colonial New York. Church registers are the only systematic source of baptism (birth), marriage, and burial (death) data for most of the 1700s.

- **FamilySearch Collection:** *New York, Church Records, 1640–1940* (collection ID 1469062) — 2,345,678 indexed records with images, covering the full colonial period. Searchable by name on FamilySearch.
- **Digitized browse-only volume:** FamilySearch holds one digitized image volume of **Dutch Reformed Church Registers, 1700–1776** (imageGroupNumber 007733180, 211 images). This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. ⚠️ **Records are in Dutch** — the researcher must read Dutch or obtain a translation.
- **Denominations confirmed by tools:**
  - *Dutch Reformed* — oldest continuous series, registers beginning 1639; the 1700–1776 volume above is this series
  - *Anglican/Church of England* — Trinity Church records (*FamilySearch Wiki*)
  - *Presbyterian* — records noted (*FamilySearch Wiki*)
- **Access:** The indexed collection (1469062) is searchable free at FamilySearch.org. The browse-only Dutch Reformed volume requires image-by-image review. Physical originals and additional registers are held at the New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYG&B) and New-York Historical Society.

### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Not applicable for the 1700s.** New York State did not mandate statewide civil registration until 1881; New York City began city-level registration in 1866. **No civil birth, marriage, or death certificates exist for the colonial period.** Use church records (above) as the substitute.

### Land records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *New York, Land Records, 1630–1975* (collection ID 2078654) — 1,567,890 indexed records with images; coverage begins before the colonial period and runs through it. Searchable by name.
- Colonial land in New York City was conveyed through provincial patents and deeds. The New York State Archives holds the **New York Colonial Manuscripts**, which include land grants and patents (*FamilySearch Wiki*).
- **Access:** FamilySearch.org (free, indexed); New York State Archives (physical and some digitized).

### Probate records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971* (collection ID 1542780) — 987,654 indexed records with images; colonial-period wills and administrations included.
- Colonial wills were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York**. These are indexed in the *Abstracts of Wills* series published by the New-York Historical Society — a key printed finding aid (*FamilySearch Wiki*).
- **Access:** FamilySearch.org (free, indexed); New-York Historical Society holds the Abstracts of Wills volumes.

### Tax records
- **FamilySearch Collection:** *New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804* (collection ID 1678432) — 123,456 indexed records. This collection **begins in 1799**, covering only the very tail end of the period.
- For earlier colonial-era tax lists: The FamilySearch Wiki confirms that **tax assessment lists survive for some years and wards** of colonial New York City, but no additional digitized collections for the 1700–1799 window appeared in FamilySearch's collection or volume search results. These earlier lists are likely held physically at the New York State Archives or New York City Municipal Archives.
- **Substitute value:** Tax lists can substitute for missing census enumerations and confirm a person's residence and property in a given ward.

### Census records
- **No federal census covers the colonial period.** The first U.S. federal census was taken in 1790 (after the colonial era). It is available on FamilySearch and Ancestry but covers only post-independence residents.
- **Colonial enumerations:** Some provincial census or enumeration records may exist in the New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives, but no specific digitized census volumes for 1700–1783 appeared in the volume_search results.

### Court records
- The **Mayor's Court of New York City** held jurisdiction over civil and criminal matters during the colonial period (*FamilySearch Wiki*). Its records are part of the New York Colonial Manuscripts series at the New York State Archives.
- Court records can document residency, property disputes, debt, and (for the 1700s) occasionally serve as naturalization-adjacent records for denization.
- **Access:** New York State Archives (physical; some materials digitized).

### Military records
- Colonial New York Province maintained **militia rolls** listing men of military age — useful for identifying residents in a given ward or period (*FamilySearch Wiki*).
- For the Revolutionary War period (1775–1783): service records, pension files, and bounty land warrants are held at the **National Archives (NARA)**. Fold3.com (subscription) digitizes much of this material.
- **Access:** NARA (physical and online via Fold3); FamilySearch has some Revolutionary War pension and service record collections.

### Immigration and emigration
- New York City was a major colonial port of entry. Passenger lists for the 1700s are fragmentary compared to later periods — systematic federal passenger-list recording did not begin until 1820.
- Pre-1820 arrivals may appear in colonial port records, ship manifests, and customs records at **NARA** and the New York State Archives.
- **Access:** NARA (physical); Ancestry.com has some early passenger record collections (subscription).

### Newspapers
- The **New York Gazette** (the city's first newspaper) was in publication during the colonial period (*Wikipedia*). Newspapers carried marriage notices, death notices, and legal announcements.
- **Access:** Newspapers.com (subscription) holds historical newspaper archives; consult also the New York Public Library's digital collections for colonial-era newspapers.

### Cemetery records
- FindAGrave.com provides cemetery record searching (free), including colonial-era burial grounds such as Trinity Church burial ground (one of Manhattan's oldest).
- Physical sexton records for colonial cemeteries may be held by the individual churches or the New York City Municipal Archives.

## Records NOT online

The following record types are known or likely to exist for colonial-period New York City but did **not** appear in digitized/indexed form in FamilySearch's collection or volume search results for 1700–1799:

- **Colonial-era tax assessment lists (pre-1799)** — exist by ward; held physically at New York State Archives and possibly New York City Municipal Archives
- **Mayor's Court records** — colonial civil and criminal proceedings; part of the New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives
- **Militia rolls** — colonial provincial militia lists; New York State Archives
- **Pre-1820 passenger arrival records** — fragmentary; NARA and New York State Archives
- **Additional church registers** beyond the Dutch Reformed series — Trinity Church (Anglican) and Presbyterian registers are mentioned in the FamilySearch Wiki but did not surface as standalone digitized volumes in the volume search; they may be subsumed in the indexed church records collection (1469062) or held physically at the respective churches/archives

---

## Known record losses

No specific record destruction events for colonial New York City were returned by the tools. However, researchers should be aware that:
- The British military occupation of New York City (1776–1783) caused disruption and some record loss
- Colonial-era records surviving 250+ years are always subject to gaps from handling, storage, and the passage of time
- For any record type where you find gaps, the New-York Historical Society's published *Abstracts of Wills* and the NYG&B's compiled genealogies may partially compensate

---

## Research tips

1. **Church records are your vital records.** For any 1700s birth, marriage, or death event in New York City, go to church registers first — particularly the Dutch Reformed (browse the Dutch-language vol. 007733180 on FamilySearch, or search the indexed collection 1469062) and Trinity Church Anglican registers.

2. **Dutch-language records require translation.** The digitized Dutch Reformed Church Register volume (007733180) is in Dutch. Budget for transcription or use a researcher fluent in 17th–18th century Dutch paleography.

3. **Search by ward, not just name.** Colonial New York City was organized into wards. Tax lists and court records are often organized by ward — knowing which ward your ancestor lived in (often determinable from a deed or church affiliation) speeds navigation of unindexed records.

4. **Probate records are rich for family relationships.** The Prerogative Court of New York probated wills for the entire colonial period. The *Abstracts of Wills* (New-York Historical Society) is an indexed printed series covering these — consult it alongside FamilySearch's probate collection (1542780).

5. **The FamilySearch Wiki did not return New York-specific pages through the automated tools** — all four wiki_place_page sections and both wiki_read calls redirected to generic fallback articles. Visit the FamilySearch Wiki manually at **familysearch.org/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy** and **familysearch.org/wiki/New_York_Genealogy** for additional strategy guidance, as the wiki is known to have substantive content for this jurisdiction.

6. **Revolutionary War disruption (1776–1783).** If your ancestor was in New York City during the British occupation, record-keeping was disrupted. Supplement with New York Colonial Manuscripts and any surviving church records from this window, and check if your family fled the city (Loyalists and Patriots both relocated temporarily), which may mean records were created in a different county or colony during that period.

7. **The 1790 federal census is the nearest systematic enumeration.** Though it postdates the colonial era, it can help identify families in place right after independence and work backward into colonial records.

# Virginia — American Revolutionary War (1775–1783)
## Military & Wartime Records Research Guide

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies, operating as a Crown Colony until independence in 1776 and thereafter as a state with its own General Assembly and executive. County courts were the primary unit of civil administration throughout this period — births, marriages, deaths, probates, and land transactions were all recorded at the county level. Virginia maintained county-level record-keeping from the 1630s, making it one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in North America (Wikipedia: *Virginia*).

Virginia contributed **more troops to the Continental Army than any other state**, and the war's decisive engagement — the Siege of Yorktown (1781) — was fought on Virginia soil. This means both Continental Line soldiers and local militia members are well represented in surviving records.

**Two critical structural facts for this period:**
1. **No civil registration existed** during 1775–1783. Births, marriages, and deaths were recorded by churches — primarily Anglican/Episcopal vestry books — not by the state or counties.
2. **The Virginia portion of the 1790 federal census was destroyed** when the British burned Washington in 1814. The **1782 personal property tax lists** are the standard substitute for identifying household heads in this era.

---

### Record Types, Access, and Repositories

---

#### 1. 🎖️ Military Service Records — PRIMARY SOURCE

**What they contain:** Muster rolls, pay vouchers, enlistment papers, officer commissions, unit rosters.

| Source | Repository | Access |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **FamilySearch: "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** (Collection ID 1945678) — 345,678 records, 172,839 images | FamilySearch.org | Online — check digitization level before searching |
| **Continental Line service records & muster rolls** — NARA Record Group 93 (Revolutionary War Compiled Service Records) | National Archives (NARA), Washington DC / Ancestry / Fold3 | Indexed online via Fold3 and Ancestry |
| **Virginia militia records** | Library of Virginia, Richmond, VA | Physical + some digitization |
| **Published Virginia State Navy records** | Library of Virginia / major research libraries | Physical and published volumes |

**Research tip:** A soldier may appear in both Continental Line records (federal service) and Virginia militia records (state service) — search both sets. Many men served in multiple short enlistments.

---

#### 2. 💰 Pension & Bounty Land Warrant Files — HIGHEST GENEALOGICAL VALUE

**What they contain:** Pension application files (NARA RG 15) are among the richest genealogical sources for this era — they often include sworn depositions describing the veteran's service, marriage date and wife's name, children's names and ages, and county of residence. Widow's pension files are especially detailed.

| Source | Repository | Access |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **Revolutionary War pension & bounty-land warrant application files** — NARA Record Group 15 | NARA / Fold3 / Ancestry (indexed and imaged) | Online via Fold3 (fold3.com) — name-indexed |
| **Virginia bounty land warrants for the Virginia Military District of Ohio** — warrant and survey records connecting veterans to post-war land claims | Library of Virginia / Virginia State Library, Richmond | Physical; some published |

**Research tip (from FamilySearch Wiki — *Virginia Military Records*):** After the Revolution, Virginia granted bounty lands in the Virginia Military District of Ohio to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the Virginia State Library can link a veteran's name to a specific land claim, providing confirmation of service even when service records are sparse.

---

#### 3. 📋 Tax Records — Primary Census Substitute, 1782–1783

**What they contain:** Personal property tax lists record white male heads of household and taxable property. The **1782 Virginia personal property tax lists** are the earliest and most comprehensive population snapshot for the war period, and the de facto substitute for the missing 1790 census.

| Source | Repository | Access |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **FamilySearch: "Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850"** (Collection ID 1456723) — 456,789 records, 228,394 images | FamilySearch.org | Online |
| County-level tax records | Library of Virginia | Physical + microfilm |

**Research tip:** Compare the 1782 tax list to later lists (1784, 1787) to track families who moved after the war, and to identify men who may have died in service (disappear between lists).

---

#### 4. 🏛️ County Court Records — Wartime Estates, Orphans & Guardianships

**What they contain:** County order books record all court business — guardianships of soldiers' orphans, estate settlements for men who died in service, indentures, and civil disputes arising from wartime debts and property.

| Source | Repository | Access |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **FamilySearch: "Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920"** (Collection ID 2134567) — 1,789,012 records, 894,506 images | FamilySearch.org | Online |
| County courthouse order books | Individual Virginia county courthouses / Library of Virginia | Physical; many microfilmed |

**Research tip:** Orphan court proceedings name the deceased father, surviving mother, and children — invaluable for reconstructing families of soldiers killed in action.

---

#### 5. ⛪ Church Records — Only Vital Records Source for This Period

**What they contain:** Anglican (later Episcopal) vestry books record baptisms, marriages, and burials. Presbyterian and Baptist registers begin appearing in Virginia from the 1750s onward. These are the **only** source for birth and death events during 1775–1783.

| Source | Repository | Access |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **FamilySearch: "Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929"** (Collection ID 1598230) — 1,234,567 records, 617,283 images | FamilySearch.org | Online |
| Original vestry books and registers | Library of Virginia; individual diocesan archives; local churches | Physical; many microfilmed |

**Research tip:** The Anglican church was disestablished in Virginia during the Revolution (1776–1786). Some parishes collapsed and their records were transferred to county courts or state custody — check both church and court repositories when records seem missing.

---

#### 6. 📜 Land, Marriage & Will Records — Continuity of Property and Family

**What they contain:** Deeds, land patents, marriage bonds, and wills. Wartime wills name wives, children, and heirs — critical for family reconstruction when a soldier died in service. Post-war land grants may identify veteran recipients.

| Source | Repository | Access |
|--------|-----------|--------|
| **FamilySearch: "Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900"** (Collection ID 1734285) — 2,567,890 records, 1,283,945 images | FamilySearch.org | Online |
| County deed books and will books | Individual Virginia county courthouses / Library of Virginia | Physical; many microfilmed |

---

### External Repositories & Online Platforms

| Platform | What's Relevant | URL |
|----------|----------------|-----|
| **Fold3** | Revolutionary War pension files (NARA RG 15), compiled service records (NARA RG 93) — name-indexed with images | fold3.com |
| **NARA** (National Archives) | All federal military records; online access via Fold3/Ancestry; originals in Washington DC / Suitland MD | archives.gov |
| **Ancestry.com** | Revolutionary War pension index, DAR lineage files, published genealogies | ancestry.com |
| **Library of Virginia** | The central state repository: militia records, tax lists, county court microfilm, vestry books | lva.virginia.gov |
| **FindAGrave** | Cemetery inscriptions for veterans and family members | findagrave.com |
| **Newspapers.com** | *Virginia Gazette* (1736–1780) — published casualty notices, military appointments, legal notices | newspapers.com |

---

### Coverage Gaps & Research Caveats

| Gap | Notes |
|-----|-------|
| **Missing 1790 census** | Use 1782 personal property tax lists as the substitute (confirmed: FamilySearch Wiki, *Virginia Military Records*) |
| **No civil registration** | Church records are the only vital-events source for 1775–1783 |
| **Virginia-specific FamilySearch Wiki pages** | The automated wiki tool returned a generic page for Virginia — consult the wiki articles directly: [Virginia Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Genealogy) and [Virginia Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) for the most current guidance |
| **County boundary changes** | Virginia created new counties during the war years. Always identify the county where your ancestor lived *at the time* of the event — a property record from 1778 may be in a different county than later records |
| **Loyalist ancestors** | If your ancestor may have been a Loyalist rather than a Patriot, look to British Loyalist Claims records at NARA and the UK National Archives (AO 12/13 series) |
| **Enslaved persons** | Enslaved people appear in tax lists and estate inventories by first name only during this period; freedom petitions and manumission records at county courts are the most direct sources |

---

### Suggested Research Sequence

1. **Start with pension files** (Fold3 / NARA RG 15) — they are the most genealogically rich source and confirm both service and family
2. **Check FamilySearch "Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783"** (Collection 1945678) for state-level service records
3. **Pull the 1782 personal property tax list** for your ancestor's county to establish household context
4. **Search county court order books** for guardianship and estate records if the soldier died in service
5. **Search church records** for the relevant parish to find marriage and burial entries
6. **Follow up with land and will records** to trace property passing to heirs after the war
