# Locality Guide: Chicago, Cook County, Illinois — Great Chicago Fire (ca. 1860–1885)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **County formed** | Cook County organized 1831 from unorganized Northwest Territory |
| **City incorporated** | Chicago incorporated as a city 1837 |
| **County seat** | Chicago |
| **Parent jurisdiction** | Illinois (admitted to statehood 1818) |
| **Population during period** | No census data returned by the place_population tool for this fixture; Chicago grew rapidly in this era as a railroad and meatpacking hub |
| **Economy** | Meatpacking, grain trade, lumber, railroads, manufacturing |
| **Ethnic composition** | Heavy immigration — Irish, German, Scandinavian, Polish, Czech, and other Central/Eastern European communities |
| **Religious denominations** | Roman Catholic, Lutheran, Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Jewish congregations, and numerous immigrant ethnic parishes |
| **Key historical event** | **Great Chicago Fire, October 8–10, 1871** — destroyed ~3.3 square miles, killed approximately 300 people, left 100,000+ homeless, and burned the Cook County Courthouse with most of the city's accumulated official records |

---

## ⚠️ The Great Fire — Record Loss (Critical Context for All Research)

The fire burned the Cook County Courthouse on October 8–10, 1871, destroying:
- Deed books and land transfer records
- Probate files (wills, estate inventories, guardianship records)
- Civil and criminal court records
- City and county tax rolls
- Many church registers for congregations whose buildings burned

This is the defining fact for Chicago genealogy before 1872: **most pre-fire official county records no longer exist in original form.** Research strategy shifts fundamentally to substitute and reconstructed sources (see Research Tips below).

*(Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire"; FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire")*

---

## Boundary changes

Cook County boundaries were essentially stable through the 1871–1885 period. No boundary changes directly affected record jurisdiction during the target window. Illinois was a federal-land state, so land patents originated with the federal General Land Office (GLO) before passing into private hands via county deed books — the county deed books were destroyed in the fire, but GLO patents predating them survive at the federal level.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

| Collection | Date range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cook County Birth Certificates | 1871–1940 | 1,450,000 | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch, collection 2024189) |
| Cook County Death Records | 1871–1947 | 980,000 | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch, collection 1913456) |
| Cook County Marriage Records | 1871–1920 | 620,000 | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch, collection 1756321) |

**Start date:** Cook County civil vital records effectively begin in 1871 (coinciding with the fire's aftermath and reconstruction). Illinois did not mandate *statewide* vital registration until 1877; pre-1877 coverage at the county level can be incomplete.

**Pre-fire / pre-registration alternative:** Church records are the primary substitute for vital events before 1871 (see Church Records below).

**Gap:** Pre-1871 civil vital records were destroyed in the fire. Do not expect to find Cook County birth, marriage, or death registrations before October 1871 in any surviving official series.

---

### Church records

| Collection | Date range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| Illinois, Cook County, Chicago Church Records | 1833–1925 | 285,000 | **Indexed + images** (FamilySearch, collection 1803978) |

**Denominations present:** Roman Catholic (multiple ethnic parishes — Irish, German, Polish, Czech, Italian), Lutheran (German and Scandinavian branches), Methodist, Presbyterian, Baptist, Episcopal, Jewish congregations.

**Survival note:** Many church registers burned with their buildings in the fire. However, some parishes kept duplicate registers or had already transferred records to diocesan archives before 1871. The FamilySearch collection (1833–1925, 285,000 records) represents those that survived and were microfilmed.

**Archdiocese of Chicago archives:** The Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives and Records Center holds Catholic parish registers not fully digitized online. Contact directly for pre-fire Catholic records; some parishes rebuilt registers from memory and sacramental testimony after the fire.

**Language:** German-language parishes kept registers in German; Polish, Czech, and other immigrant congregations used their heritage languages. Expect non-English records for ethnic parishes through at least the 1880s.

---

### Census records

| Census year | Status |
|---|---|
| 1850 federal | Survived — available on FamilySearch and Ancestry, indexed |
| 1860 federal | Survived — available on FamilySearch and Ancestry, indexed |
| **1870 federal** | **Survived — this is the last pre-fire enumeration and critically important**; originals were in Washington, D.C. and thus escaped the fire |
| 1880 federal | Survived — available on FamilySearch, indexed |
| 1900 federal | Survived (no 1890 for Chicago — the 1890 federal census was largely destroyed in a 1921 fire at NARA) |
| Illinois state censuses | Illinois held state censuses in 1855, 1865, 1885 — coverage and survival vary; check the Illinois State Archives |
| Mortality schedules | Available for 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 — record deaths in the year prior to enumeration; valuable for tracing fire victims near 1870–1871 |

**Research priority:** The **1870 federal census** is the single most important substitute source for families living in Chicago immediately before the fire. It was enumerated just one year before the disaster and names every household member.

---

### Probate and court records

| Volume | Date range | Images | Access level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pre-fire County Court Records (reconstructed copies) — IGN 009982110 | 1865–1871 | 38 | **Browse-only images** — 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable; must be browsed image by image |
| Post-fire Property Re-recordings — IGN 009982111 | 1871–1880 | 112 | **Partially indexed + images** — 41% name-indexed; remaining 59% requires browsing |

**Original pre-fire probate and court records were destroyed in the fire.** The 38-image volume (IGN 009982110) contains reconstructed copies filed afterward — these are derivative records, not originals. Treat information in them accordingly.

**Post-fire court records** from the Cook County Circuit Court are held at the Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD) at Northeastern Illinois University, Chicago.

---

### Land records

**⚠️ Most pre-fire deed books were destroyed in the fire.** Two substitute strategies exist:

1. **Burnt Record Act of 1872:** Illinois law required property owners to re-register their deeds. These reconstructed deed filings are the primary post-fire substitute for pre-fire property ownership. The partially-indexed Post-fire Property Re-recordings volume on FamilySearch (IGN 009982111, 1871–1880, 112 images, 41% indexed) is the digitized portion of this series.

2. **Chicago Title and Trust Company records:** Insurance company records documenting property ownership became vital substitutes. This collection is held at the **Chicago History Museum** (physical access; not fully online). *(Source: Wikipedia, "Great Chicago Fire")*

3. **Federal GLO patents:** Land patents issued before the private deed chain (federal-land state system) survive at the Bureau of Land Management's General Land Office website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) and predate the destroyed county deed books.

---

### Military records

**Relevant conflict:** The Civil War (1861–1865) preceded the fire; Illinois regiments were heavily recruited from Cook County. Pre-fire service records and pension files were held federally at NARA and **survived** — the fire did not affect federal military archives.

| Record type | Where held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Civil War service records | NARA (Washington, D.C.) | Fold3 (subscription) — indexed + images |
| Civil War pension files | NARA | Fold3, or order directly from NARA — physical |
| Draft registrations (Civil War) | NARA / Fold3 | Indexed + images |
| Illinois Adjutant General records | Illinois State Archives, Springfield | Physical / some online finding aids |

---

### Cemetery records

Major Chicago-area cemeteries active in 1871 include Graceland Cemetery (est. 1860), Rosehill Cemetery (est. 1859), and St. Boniface (Catholic, German). Many ethnic and denominational cemeteries operated independently.

- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) — online, searchable; coverage varies by cemetery and volunteer contribution
- **Sexton / burial records:** Physical registers held by individual cemeteries and the Cook County Clerk — not fully digitized

---

### Newspaper records

The **Chicago Tribune** (founded 1847) and **Chicago Inter Ocean** survived the fire and provided extensive coverage of the disaster, including lists of the dead, missing, and homeless. Newspaper notices for deaths, marriages, property sales, and legal notices are a key substitute source when official records are absent.

- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) — historical Chicago newspapers, searchable full text
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free) — some Illinois papers digitized for this period
- **Newberry Library**, Chicago — holds microfilm of many Chicago-area newspapers; in-person access

---

### Immigration and naturalization records

Chicago was a major destination for immigrant waves in the 1860s–1880s — Irish, German, Scandinavian, Polish, Czech, and others. The fire did not affect federal immigration records.

| Record type | Where held | Access |
|---|---|---|
| Passenger arrival lists | NARA; Ancestry; FamilySearch | Indexed + images (Ancestry most comprehensive) |
| Naturalization records (pre-1906) | Scattered across Cook County Circuit Court, federal courts — originals at IRAD / NARA | Partially indexed; some browse-only |
| Soundex index to naturalizations | NARA Great Lakes Region, Chicago | Physical |

**Note:** Pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in any court of record — county, state, or federal. Cook County Circuit Court naturalization files that survived the fire are held at IRAD at Northeastern Illinois University. Check all three court levels.

**Passenger lists record all family members**, including infants and young children traveling with parents. When tracing an immigrant family, review the full manifest page for siblings and other relatives traveling together.

---

### Tax records

Pre-fire tax rolls were destroyed. Post-fire property tax records from Cook County are held at the Cook County Assessor's office and IRAD; these are largely **physical only**. Tax records can substitute for census years — the 1872–1874 tax rolls are particularly useful for confirming post-fire residence and property reconstruction.

---

### City directories

Chicago city directories from the **1840s onward survived the fire** and are held at the **Newberry Library**. They are one of the best substitutes for destroyed vital and property records, providing annual snapshots of residents, occupations, and addresses. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki, "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy — Record Loss and the Great Fire")*

Some pre-1871 Chicago directories have been digitized and are browsable through the **Newberry Library's digital collections** and **Ancestry**.

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Cook County Church Records 1833–1925 (285K); Birth Certificates 1871–1940 (1.45M); Death Records 1871–1947 (980K); Marriage Records 1871–1920 (620K); Pre-fire Court Records vol. (38 images, browse-only); Post-fire Property Re-recordings vol. (112 images, 41% indexed) | Free |
| **Ancestry** | Federal census (1850, 1860, 1870, 1880); Civil War records; city directories; some Cook County records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Civil War service records and pension files; draft registrations | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Chicago Tribune and other Illinois papers | Subscription |
| **Chronicling America (LOC)** | Some Illinois newspapers, free | Free |
| **BLM GLO** | Federal land patents (pre-deed chain) | Free |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery memorial records | Free |

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Key holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Newberry Library**, Chicago | City directories (1840s+), maps, manuscripts, ethnic research collections | In-person; some materials digitized |
| **Chicago History Museum** | Chicago Title and Trust insurance records; photographs; personal papers of fire survivors | In-person; contact for access |
| **Illinois Regional Archives Depository (IRAD), Northeastern Illinois University** | Cook County court records post-1871; surviving pre-fire reconstructed records; naturalization files | In-person; some finding aids online |
| **Archdiocese of Chicago — Joseph Cardinal Bernardin Archives** | Catholic parish registers (pre- and post-fire) | Contact archives directly |
| **Cook County Clerk's Office** | Vital records from 1871; deed records post-Burnt Record Act | In-person / mail; some records via online portals |
| **Illinois State Archives, Springfield** | State census records (1855, 1865, 1885); state-level military records; land records | In-person; some online finding aids |
| **NARA Great Lakes Region, Chicago** | Federal naturalization records; federal court records; some census originals | In-person |

---

## Records NOT online

The following records exist but are **not available in any online database** — they require in-person or mail access:

- **Chicago Title and Trust Company insurance records** (Chicago History Museum) — key substitute for destroyed pre-fire deeds
- **Cook County pre-fire reconstructed probate files** beyond the 38-image FamilySearch volume
- **Catholic parish registers** not included in the FamilySearch church records collection (Bernardin Archives)
- **Cook County post-fire naturalization files** (IRAD — partial finding aids only)
- **City and county tax rolls** (post-fire, 1872 onward — Cook County Assessor / IRAD)
- **Cook County Circuit Court case files** post-1871 in full (IRAD)
- **Cemetery sexton / burial registers** for most individual cemeteries

---

## Known record losses

| Event | Date | What was lost | Substitute sources |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Great Chicago Fire** | Oct 8–10, 1871 | Cook County Courthouse contents: deed books, probate files, court records, tax rolls; many church registers | Burnt Record Act reconstructed deeds; 1870 federal census; city directories (Newberry); Chicago Title & Trust insurance records (Chicago History Museum); surviving church registers (Bernardin Archives); federal GLO patents |
| **1890 federal census** | Fire at NARA, 1921 | Nationwide — the 1890 census for Chicago (and the country) is largely destroyed | 1885 Illinois state census; 1891–1900 city directories; Cook County vital records (1871+) for the intervening decade |

---

## Research tips

1. **Start with the 1870 federal census.** It's the last pre-fire snapshot of Chicago households, enumerated just one year before the disaster, and it survived because the originals were held in Washington. This is your anchor.

2. **Work the Burnt Record Act files for property.** The Post-fire Property Re-recordings volume on FamilySearch (IGN 009982111, 1871–1880) is only 41% name-indexed — browse all 112 images if your name search fails. The Cook County Recorder and IRAD hold the broader series.

3. **Use city directories as a substitute vital record.** Annual Chicago city directories (1840s onward) at the Newberry Library survive intact and provide year-by-year residence, occupation, and address information. A gap or appearance in the directory can bracket a birth, death, or move.

4. **Pursue church records through the Bernardin Archives** for Catholic families, especially immigrant ethnic parishes. The diocesan archives held records that individual parish buildings did not, and some parishes reconstructed their registers from memory and sacramental testimony after the fire.

5. **Chicago Title and Trust records are a key substitute for deeds.** The insurance company's pre-fire documentation of property ownership (now at the Chicago History Museum) was specifically noted by Wikipedia's Great Chicago Fire article as a vital substitute for destroyed Cook County deeds. Plan an in-person or correspondence visit.

6. **Do not assume pre-fire records are gone without checking every substitute.** The fire destroyed the *courthouse*, not *all* records touching Chicago. Federal census originals, military records at NARA, federal land patents, and records held by parishes, insurers, and individuals all survived.

7. **For immigrant families:** Naturalization files scattered across county, state, and federal courts — check IRAD, the NARA Great Lakes Region, and FamilySearch for overlapping coverage. Heavy immigration from Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia, Poland, and Bohemia means ethnic parish registers and foreign-language newspapers may be the only pre-fire documentary trail.

8. **Browse the pre-fire reconstructed court records** (FamilySearch IGN 009982110, 1865–1871, 38 images) image by image — this volume is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. It is the only digitized window into pre-fire Cook County court proceedings.

9. **Consult the FamilySearch Wiki article** "Cook County, Illinois Genealogy" (https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Cook_County,_Illinois_Genealogy) for further repository contact details and research strategies specific to the fire's impact.

---

## 📜 Locality Research Guide: Louisiana — French Colonial Period (1700s)

### Jurisdictional Context

**French Louisiana (La Louisiane)** was a district of New France, administered by France from **1699 to 1762**, when France secretly ceded the territory west of the Mississippi to Spain in the Treaty of Fontainebleau. Spain did not take physical administrative control until **1769**, so the practical boundary of the "French period" is **1699–1769**. New Orleans was founded in 1718 by Jean-Baptiste Le Moyne de Bienville and became the colonial capital.

**Key implication for researchers:** Families living through the 1760s straddle a jurisdictional handoff. Records created before ~1769 follow French administrative forms (in French); records after 1769 shift to Spanish administration. Treat French and early Spanish colonial records as **one continuous research trail** — do not research one period without checking the other. *(Spain held the colony until 1800, when it was secretly retroceded to France; Napoleon then sold it to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.)*

---

### Record Types, Repositories & Access

#### 1. 🏛️ Catholic Parish Registers — **PRIMARY SOURCE**
*Baptisms · Marriages · Burials*

The Catholic Church was the **only legally recognized church** in French Louisiana. Parish registers are the closest equivalent to vital records for this period. The *Code Noir* (Black Code) required the Catholic baptism of all enslaved persons, so registers may also document enslaved individuals and, indirectly, their families.

- **St. Louis Cathedral, New Orleans** holds registers from **1720** — the earliest surviving sacramental records for the colony.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905) (Collection ID 1612905) — **directly covers the French period from 1718**. FamilySearch reports ~987,654 indexed records and ~493,827 images, indicating this collection is **indexed with images**.
- ⚠️ **Language warning:** All entries are in 18th-century French, written in cursive *écriture courante*. Researchers must read French or work with a translator/paleographer.
- Also check individual parish archives and the **Archdiocese of New Orleans** for registers not yet digitized.

---

#### 2. ⚖️ Superior Council Records (Conseil Supérieur)
*Land grants · Court proceedings · Contracts · Estate inventories*

The Superior Council was the colony's governing and judicial body. Its records are the French-period equivalent of county court files and include:
- **Concessions (land grants)** — the primary form of land tenure
- **Estate inventories** — often naming family members, relationships, and property
- **Civil and criminal court proceedings**
- **Marriage contracts** (separate from church registers — often held notarially)

**Where held:** The **Louisiana Historical Center**, located in the Old U.S. Mint building in New Orleans, holds these records and has partially digitized them. Contact the center directly for access details.

- ⚠️ **Language warning:** Records are in French.
- **FamilySearch collection:** [Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341) (Collection ID 2078341) begins in **1756**, covering the last decade of French control. ~456,789 indexed records and ~228,394 images — **indexed with images**.

---

#### 3. 📝 Notarial Records
*Contracts · Wills · Marriage settlements · Property transactions*

The **New Orleans Notarial Archives** is the oldest continuously operating notarial office in North America. Holdings go back to the **1730s** and include:
- Marriage contracts (distinct from church registers)
- Wills and succession documents
- Property sale and transfer contracts
- Manumission documents (freeing of enslaved persons)

**Access:** The **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** is open to the public. Many early volumes are on microfilm; digitization is ongoing.

- ⚠️ All early records are in French.

---

#### 4. 🌾 Land Records & Concessions
*French land grants · American State Papers*

French colonial land tenure was based on *concessions* (grants from the Crown), not English common law. Key sources:

- **American State Papers: Public Lands** — documents French and Spanish colonial land grants as they were adjudicated after the Louisiana Purchase. Widely available in print and on HathiTrust/Google Books.
- **Louisiana State Land Office** — holds records of original land grants confirmed after 1803.
- **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM), Aix-en-Provence, France** — holds the original French administrative correspondence and some land grant documentation. See below.

---

#### 5. 📋 Colonial Census Rolls (*Recensements*)
*Population lists · Household enumerations*

France conducted periodic census-style enumerations of the Louisiana colony. These list heads of household and sometimes family members, servants, and enslaved persons.

**Where held:** The **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** in Aix-en-Provence, France, holds colonial administrative correspondence and *recensements*. Some have been microfilmed and are accessible through ANOM's online catalog ([anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr](https://anom.archivesnationales.culture.gouv.fr)).

- These are not currently in FamilySearch's indexed collections but are a critical source for pre-1720 and early settlement research.

---

#### 6. 🔍 Other Sources to Search

| Record Type | Where Held | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Military service (French colonial troops) | ANOM (France); Louisiana Historical Center | Soldiers, officers, and militia |
| Ship passenger lists | ANOM; Louisiana Historical Center | French immigration to the colony |
| Indenture/engagés records | ANOM | Indentured workers (engagés) sent to the colony |
| Cemetery records | Find A Grave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com)) | Some colonial-era grave markers survive |
| Newspaper records (post-1764) | Tulane University; Louisiana State University | *La Gazette de la Louisiane* and successors |
| Published abstracts & transcriptions | Genealogical Society of Southwestern Louisiana; Louisiana Genealogical & Historical Society | Many colonial records have been abstracted in print |

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Online Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Church records (from 1718), probate records (from 1756) | [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) — indexed + images |
| **Louisiana Historical Center** (Old U.S. Mint, New Orleans) | Superior Council records, colonial documents | Partial digitization; in-person / contact center |
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | Notarial acts from 1730s | In-person; some microfilm |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)** (Aix-en-Provence, France) | Colonial admin records, census rolls, ship lists | Online catalog + some digitized images |
| **Louisiana State Archives** (Baton Rouge) | State-era records; some colonial-period carryovers | [sos.la.gov/HistoricalResources](https://www.sos.la.gov/HistoricalResources) |
| **NARA** | American State Papers (Land); post-1803 federal records | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |

---

### Researcher Warnings & Quirks

1. **All French-period records are in French.** Church registers, notarial acts, Superior Council files, and colonial correspondence are written in 18th-century cursive French (*écriture courante*). Budget time for translation or hire a specialist.

2. **French → Spanish transition (~1762–1769).** The Treaty of Fontainebleau (1762) ended French sovereignty, but Spain didn't physically govern until 1769. Records from the 1760s may be administratively French but show transitional forms. Always search both French and early Spanish colonial records as a connected trail.

3. **No civil registration in this period.** The U.S. *Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964* (Collection 1543892) and *Louisiana, Parish Marriages, 1837–1957* (Collection 1798054) on FamilySearch are both **post-colonial** and do **not** cover the 1700s. Do not expect them to appear for this research window.

4. **Catholic baptism = the birth record.** There are no civil birth registers. The baptismal entry in a parish register is the primary evidence of birth. The same logic applies to burials and marriage acts.

5. **Enslaved persons.** The *Code Noir* mandated Catholic baptism of enslaved people. Parish registers are often the **only documentary trace** for enslaved individuals in this period. Estate inventories (in Superior Council / probate records) may also name them.

6. **ANOM requires patience.** The French national archives overseas collection is rich but not fully digitized. Some series require an in-person visit or a hired researcher in Aix-en-Provence. Check ANOM's online catalog first to identify relevant series (notably the *Colonies* series, sub-series G1).

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Availability | Access Level |
|---|---|---|
| Church records (baptism/marriage/burial), 1718+ | Collection 1612905 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Probate/estate records, 1756+ | Collection 2078341 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Superior Council records | Louisiana Historical Center | ⚠️ Partial digitization — browse/physical |
| Notarial acts, 1730s+ | Notarial Archives Research Center | ⚠️ Microfilm / in-person |
| Colonial census rolls (*recensements*) | ANOM (France) | ⚠️ Partial online catalog; some digital images |
| French land concessions | American State Papers (HathiTrust); BLM GLO | ✅ Widely available in print/online |

---

**Bottom line:** The French colonial 1700s are genuinely researchable, but most of the richest records — Superior Council files, notarial acts, and ANOM material — are not fully indexed and require either in-person visits, French-language reading ability, or both. **Start with FamilySearch's church records collection (1612905)**, which is indexed from 1718 and covers the entire French period. Then extend to the notarial archives and Superior Council holdings for land, property, and estate information.

# Locality Guide: Pennsylvania Coal Mining Towns (Late 1800s, c. 1860–1900)

## Jurisdiction Overview

Pennsylvania's coal mining region divides into two geographically distinct zones, each with its own counties, ethnic communities, and record-keeping patterns:

**Anthracite (Hard Coal) Region — Northeastern Pennsylvania**
Centered on **Schuylkill** (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton), **Luzerne** (formed 1786), **Lackawanna** (formed **1878 from Luzerne**), **Carbon** (formed 1843 from Northampton and Monroe), and **Northumberland** counties. Key towns: Pottsville, Shenandoah, Mahanoy City, Wilkes-Barre, Scranton, Carbondale, Hazleton, Mauch Chunk (now Jim Thorpe).

**Bituminous (Soft Coal) Region — Southwestern Pennsylvania**
Centered on **Cambria** (formed 1804; county seat Ebensburg; includes Johnstown), **Westmoreland** (formed 1773), **Fayette**, **Indiana**, and **Washington** counties. Key towns: Johnstown, Connellsville, Uniontown, Greensburg.

- **Economy:** Coal mining dominated; ancillary iron, steel, and railroad industries
- **Ethnic composition:** Early waves — Irish, Welsh, English, German. Later waves (1880s–1900s) — Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Hungarian, Italian, Ukrainian. Each group often settled in distinct patches and patches formed their own ethnic parishes.
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic (Irish, Polish, Lithuanian, Slovak, Italian), Welsh Congregational/Presbyterian, Episcopal, Methodist, Lutheran (German), Greek Catholic (Ukrainian/Ruthenian), Jewish
- **Key historical events:** Molly Maguires trials (Schuylkill/Carbon counties, 1870s); Johnstown Flood (Cambria County, May 31, 1889); widespread labor unrest; founding of United Mine Workers of America (UMWA, 1890)

---

## Boundary Changes — Critical for Research

| County | Formed | Parent(s) | Research Implication |
|---|---|---|---|
| Schuylkill | 1811 | Berks, Northampton | Records before 1811 filed under Berks or Northampton |
| Carbon | 1843 | Northampton, Monroe | Records before 1843 in Northampton or Monroe |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878** | **Luzerne** | **Records for Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 are filed under Luzerne County — search Luzerne first** |
| Cambria | 1804 | Somerset, Huntingdon | Records before 1804 in those parent counties |
| Westmoreland | 1773 | Bedford | Pre-1773 records in Bedford |

**The Lackawanna/Luzerne split is the most consequential boundary change for late-1800s research.** Anyone living in the Scranton or Carbondale area before 1878 will have records only in Luzerne County.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)

- **Start date:** Pennsylvania did **not** require statewide civil registration of births and deaths until **January 1, 1906**. This falls entirely outside the 1860–1900 target window.
- **Marriage registration:** County-level marriage registration was inconsistently enforced before the 1880s. FamilySearch's **Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1885–1950** (collection 1921317; 524,189 records, 312,045 images) — **indexed + images** — is the primary online source for late-1800s marriages.
- **Gaps:** No statewide birth or death certificates exist for the 1860–1900 period. Church records are the only systematic source for baptisms and burials.
- **Post-period note:** FamilySearch's **Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906–1968** (collection 2255317; 4,218,763 records + images, **indexed + images**) begins in 1906. For anyone who died after that date, these certificates often record birthplace, parents' names, and informant — useful for working back into the 1880s–1890s.

### Church Records ⭐ Primary Source for This Period

Church records are the **single most important substitute** for absent civil vital records. For coal mining communities, ethnic parishes are essential — each immigrant group typically maintained its own congregation with registers in the heritage language.

- **Denominations and their record languages:**
  - Irish and later Polish/Lithuanian/Slovak/Italian: **Roman Catholic** (Latin registers; later in vernacular). Diocese of Scranton (1868) and Diocese of Allentown (from larger dioceses) cover the anthracite region. Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown covers much of the bituminous region.
  - Welsh miners: **Congregational/Presbyterian** (Welsh-language registers common in Schuylkill and Carbon counties)
  - German settlers: **Lutheran and Reformed** (German-language registers)
  - Ukrainian/Ruthenian miners (late 1880s–1900s): **Greek Catholic / Byzantine Rite** (Church Slavonic)
- **FamilySearch collection:** **Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985** (collection 1401638; 1,245,830 records, 982,415 indexed persons, 607,220 images) — **indexed + images**. This is the largest online source for pre-1906 vital-type events in Pennsylvania.
- **Also on FamilySearch:** **Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677–1950** (collection 1571957; 312,045 records, 156,023 images) — **indexed + images**; and **Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700–1900** (collection 1502909; 198,765 records, **0 images** — index only, no images viewable online).
- **Physical holdings:** Diocesan archives hold originals for Catholic parishes. Many Welsh Congregational and German Lutheran registers survive at local historical societies. FamilySearch has microfilmed many Pennsylvania church registers; check the FamilySearch Catalog by county for specific holdings not yet digitized.

### Census Records

| Census Year | Coverage | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1860 | Full federal enumeration | Indexed + images (Ancestry, FamilySearch) | Lists occupation; identifies mining families |
| 1870 | Full federal enumeration | Indexed + images | Lists birthplace and parents' birthplace |
| 1880 | Full federal enumeration | Indexed + images | Includes relationship to head of household — the most useful pre-1900 census |
| **1890** | **Largely destroyed** | — | **Fire 1921; only fragments survive. A significant gap.** |
| 1900 | Full federal enumeration | Indexed + images | Lists years in US, naturalization status, number of children |

- **Mortality schedules** (1870, 1880): List deaths in the 12 months preceding the census with age, birthplace, cause of death, and occupation. Valuable for identifying mining accident victims. Available on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **Veterans' schedules** (1880): Enumerate surviving Civil War veterans. Available on Ancestry.
- **No Pennsylvania state census** was taken during this period.
- **Tip:** The 1880 census (and later 1900) specifically listed occupation as "miner," "mine laborer," or "collier." Search by occupation as well as name when locating families in mining towns.

### Occupational Records ⭐ Distinctive to Coal Mining

These records are unique to coal country and often survive where civil vital records do not. Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Coal Mining*:

- **Mine Worker Employment Cards (Schuylkill County, 1870–1900):** FamilySearch has digitized this collection as image group **002240015** — 410 images, **95% name-indexed and full-text searchable** — the most accessible mining record set identified in the volume survey.
- **Mine Accident Reports (Luzerne County, 1870–1895):** Image group **002240016** — 287 images, **0% indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only, image by image.** These often record age, nationality, and cause of death for fatal accidents.
- **Colliery Payroll Ledgers (Lackawanna County, 1878–1900):** Image group **002240017** — 199 images, **0% indexed and not full-text searchable — browse-only.** Confirm employment and wages.
- **Note:** The volume search returned 23 total results for Pennsylvania 1860–1900 but pagination returned only the first 3 in this survey. Additional volumes likely exist for other coal counties; consult the FamilySearch Catalog directly for additional digitized volumes.
- **Mine Inspector Annual Reports (from 1870):** Published by the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania annually from 1870. Each report lists fatal accidents with miner's name, age, nationality/birthplace, and cause of death. **Physical copies held at the Pennsylvania State Archives** (Harrisburg); some years available via HathiTrust and Google Books.
- **UMWA Records:** The United Mine Workers of America (founded 1890) membership rolls and grievance files survive fragmentarily. Contact the UMWA Historical Collection at the Pennsylvania State Archives and the Historical Society of Schuylkill County.
- **Company records:** Coal company payrolls, employment records, and accident reports survive at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**, the **Historical Society of Schuylkill County** (Pottsville), and the **Anthracite Heritage Museum** (Scranton/McDade Park). Coverage is fragmentary — not all companies' records survived.

### Immigration and Naturalization Records ⭐ Critical for This Population

The vast majority of coal miners in the late 1800s were immigrants or first-generation Americans. Per the FamilySearch Wiki article *Pennsylvania Occupational Records — Mining Community Sources*:

- **Passenger lists:** Most anthracite-region immigrants entered through Philadelphia or New York. NARA holds passenger lists; indexed versions are on Ancestry (subscription) and FamilySearch (free). Lists record name, age, occupation, last residence, and destination. **Full manifest pages list all family members including infants and young children** — always examine the whole manifest page, not just the indexed entry.
- **Naturalization records (pre-1906):** Before September 27, 1906, naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — federal, state, or local. In coal counties this means county Courts of Common Pleas. Declarations of intent ("first papers") and petitions for citizenship are found at county courthouses.
  - **Schuylkill County naturalization records, 1840s–1906** are held at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**.
  - Similar records for Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Cambria, and Westmoreland counties are at their respective county courthouses or state archives.
- **Post-1906 naturalizations** were centralized through federal courts; records at NARA Philadelphia (Mid-Atlantic Region).
- **Tip:** Many miners naturalized as quickly as possible (some states required it for mine employment). Naturalization papers often state exact village of birth, arrival date, and port — details not found elsewhere.

### Probate and Court Records

- **FamilySearch collection:** **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection 1999196; 893,214 records, 446,607 images) — **indexed + images**. Wills and estate inventories reveal family relationships, property, and neighbors.
- **Physical holdings:** County Orphans' Courts (now Orphans' Court division of Court of Common Pleas) at each county courthouse.
- **Note:** Many miners owned little real property; estates may be small or administered informally. However, mining accident wrongful-death suits do appear in court records.

### Land Records

- **System:** Metes-and-bounds (Pennsylvania is a state-land state; no federal land survey). Land grants trace to the original Penn proprietorship.
- **Coal company land:** Much land in coal regions was owned by coal companies (e.g., Philadelphia and Reading Coal & Iron, Lehigh Coal & Navigation). Individual miners rented company housing; they would not appear in deed books as property owners. **Tax records** (below) are a better annual locating tool.
- **Deed books:** County Recorders of Deeds. Not consistently digitized for this period; physical access required.

### Tax Records

- **Pennsylvania county tax records** (real and personal property assessments) survive for most coal counties throughout the 1800s. Held at county archives and historical societies. Useful annual snapshots for locating a family in an intercensal year and as a substitute for the destroyed 1890 census.
- **Physical only** for most counties; some transcribed by local genealogical societies.

### Military Records

- **Civil War (1861–1865):** Pennsylvania contributed heavily. Service records and pension files at NARA (indexed on Ancestry/Fold3); Pennsylvania adjutant general records at the **Pennsylvania State Archives**; regimental histories at the State Library of Pennsylvania.
- **Spanish-American War (1898):** Service records at NARA; Pennsylvania muster rolls at the State Archives.
- **Civil War draft records (1863 Conscription Act):** Consolidated draft lists for Pennsylvania counties are at NARA (indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch) — list age, occupation, birthplace, and marital status. Valuable for men not enumerated in 1860 census.

### Cemetery Records

- **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) has extensive coverage of Pennsylvania coal region cemeteries, including many ethnic Catholic, Welsh, and Protestant burial grounds.
- **BillionGraves** provides additional headstone photograph coverage.
- **Sexton records and burial registers:** Physical records at individual cemeteries, churches, or local historical societies. Coverage varies widely. The Historical Society of Schuylkill County has transcribed many local cemeteries.
- **Note:** Mine disasters created mass burial events; local newspapers and coroners' records supplement cemetery records for accident victims.

### Newspaper Records

- **Newspapers.com** (subscription) holds many Pennsylvania coal-region papers; search for obituaries, marriage notices, accident reports, and legal notices.
- **Chronicling America** (Library of Congress, free): Digitized Pennsylvania newspapers including several from the anthracite region.
- **Notable papers:** *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville, Schuylkill County — continuous since 1825; invaluable for the entire coal region), *Scranton Tribune*, *Wilkes-Barre Record*, *Hazleton Plain Speaker*.
- **Content value:** Obituaries in coal towns routinely name the deceased's birthplace, surviving family members, and church affiliation. Mine disaster coverage names individual victims. The *Miners' Journal* covered labor disputes, accidents, and community life in extraordinary detail.

### Coroners' Records

- County coroners investigated all accidental deaths, including mine fatalities. Coroners' inquest records often name the deceased, age, nationality, witnesses, and cause of death. **Physical only** at county courthouses or archives. Not consistently digitized.

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories
| Repository | Key Collections for This Place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church & Town Records (1401638); County Marriages (1921317); Probate Records (1999196); Civil Marriages (1571957); Compiled Marriages (1502909); Mine Worker Employment Cards [Schuylkill, image group 002240015]; Mine Accident Reports [Luzerne, image group 002240016 — browse-only]; Colliery Payroll Ledgers [Lackawanna, image group 002240017 — browse-only] | Free |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses 1860–1900; Civil War service & pension records; naturalization records; Pennsylvania vital records | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | Civil War & Spanish-American War records; draft records | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Pennsylvania coal-region newspapers; obituaries, accident reports | Subscription |
| **Chronicling America** (loc.gov/chroniclingamerica) | Digitized Pennsylvania newspapers | Free |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Pennsylvania coal-region cemetery records | Free |
| **HathiTrust / Google Books** | Pennsylvania Mine Inspector annual reports (1870+) | Free |
| **NARA** (archives.gov) | Passenger lists; post-1906 naturalizations; Civil War records | Free (some via Fold3/Ancestry) |

### Physical Repositories
| Repository | Key Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Pennsylvania State Archives**, Harrisburg | Mine Inspector reports; Schuylkill County naturalizations (1840s–1906); state military records; UMWA-related records | In-person; some records by mail request |
| **Historical Society of Schuylkill County**, Pottsville | Mining company employment records; local newspapers; cemetery transcriptions; local histories | In-person |
| **Anthracite Heritage Museum**, Scranton (McDade Park) | Mining community records; ethnic community collections; photographs | In-person |
| **Lackawanna County Historical Society**, Scranton | Records for Scranton/Carbondale area post-1878 (and Luzerne County pre-1878 material) | In-person |
| **Luzerne County Historical Society**, Wilkes-Barre | Wilkes-Barre/Hazleton area records; pre-1878 Lackawanna County material | In-person |
| **Carbon County Historical Society**, Jim Thorpe | Carbon County records; Molly Maguires-related materials | In-person |
| **Cambria County Historical Society**, Ebensburg | Cambria/Johnstown area records; Johnstown Flood documentation | In-person |
| **Diocese of Scranton Archives** | Catholic parish registers for NE Pennsylvania coal region | By appointment |
| **Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown Archives** | Catholic parish registers for SW Pennsylvania coal region (Cambria, Indiana, etc.) | By appointment |
| **NARA Mid-Atlantic Region**, Philadelphia | Federal court naturalizations post-1906; federal census originals | In-person |
| **County Courthouses** (each coal county) | Deed books; naturalization records pre-1906; court of common pleas records; orphans' court | In-person |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following records **exist** but have **no meaningful online presence** and require in-person or correspondence access:

- **County tax assessment records** — at county archives/historical societies
- **Coroners' inquest records** — at county courthouses or historical societies
- **Most coal company employment records** — fragmentarily held at historical societies (no online database)
- **Pre-1906 naturalization records** for most counties other than Schuylkill (those are at the PA State Archives)
- **Diocesan Catholic parish registers** not yet microfilmed or digitized — contact individual diocesan archives
- **Welsh Congregational and smaller denominational registers** — at local churches or Welsh-American historical societies
- **UMWA membership rolls** — fragmented; at PA State Archives and historical societies
- **Mine Inspector district-level records** (as opposed to published annual reports) — at PA State Archives

---

## Known Record Losses

- **1890 Federal Census:** Largely destroyed in a 1921 fire in Washington, D.C. A significant gap for all researchers. **Substitute sources:** 1880 and 1900 censuses bracketing the period; state/county tax records; city directories; church registers; voter registrations.
- **Johnstown Flood (May 31, 1889):** The catastrophic flood in Cambria County destroyed significant local records and family documents in Johnstown and surrounding communities. Substitute sources include coroner records (extensive post-flood), Red Cross relief records, and newspapers (the disaster was nationally covered).
- **Individual courthouse records:** Some Pennsylvania county courthouses experienced partial record losses; check with specific county historical societies before assuming a record set is complete.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with church records, not civil vital records.** Pennsylvania did not require statewide registration of births and deaths until 1906. For the entire 1860–1900 window, church baptismal, marriage, and burial registers are your primary source for vital events.

2. **Identify the ethnic parish first.** A Polish miner in Shenandoah belonged to a different Catholic parish than an Irish miner on the same street. Knowing your ancestor's ethnicity tells you which parish to search. The FamilySearch collection *Pennsylvania, Church and Town Records, 1708–1985* (1401638) is the starting point, but many ethnic parishes' records are still only at diocesan archives.

3. **Lackawanna County records before 1878 are filed under Luzerne County.** If your ancestor was in Scranton, Carbondale, or the Wyoming Valley before Lackawanna County was created in 1878, search Luzerne County records for that period. Work both counties together as one continuous research trail.

4. **Mine Inspector Reports (1870+) are an underused source.** The Pennsylvania annual Mine Inspector reports name fatal accident victims with age, nationality, and cause of death — a substitute death record for miners who died on the job before 1906. Available at the PA State Archives and partially on HathiTrust/Google Books.

5. **Naturalization records are essential for immigrant miners.** Declarations of intent and petitions name exact village of origin in Europe — often the only document that does. Pre-1906 naturalizations are scattered across county courts; Schuylkill County's are at the PA State Archives. For other counties, contact the county courthouse directly.

6. **The destroyed 1890 census leaves a 20-year gap between 1880 and 1900.** Bridge it with: the 1885 or 1895 state veterans' census (if applicable), county tax lists, city directories, church records, and naturalization filings.

7. **Use the *Miners' Journal* (Pottsville).** Published continuously since 1825, it covered the entire anthracite coal region and reported mine accidents, labor disputes, community events, and obituaries with unusually rich detail. Available on Newspapers.com and partially through Chronicling America.

8. **Coal company housing records:** Many miners lived in company-owned patch towns. Company store ledgers (truck system accounts) sometimes survive and can document a family's presence at a specific location. Check the Historical Society of Schuylkill County and the Anthracite Heritage Museum.

9. **DNA evidence** can supplement the fragmentary documentary record, especially for identifying origins in specific villages in Ireland, Poland, Slovakia, or Wales when immigration records are incomplete.

10. **The FamilySearch volume survey returned 23 total volumes for Pennsylvania 1860–1900 but only 3 were returned in this survey** (Mine Worker Employment Cards, Mine Accident Reports, Colliery Payroll Ledgers). Additional digitized volumes likely exist; search the FamilySearch Catalog directly at familysearch.org/catalog by county and record type.

---

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States — Early 1600s Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1700)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Formed:** Plymouth Colony established 1620; Massachusetts Bay Colony chartered 1628, with major settlement beginning 1630 (the "Great Migration," ~20,000 settlers, 1630–1640). In **1691**, Plymouth Colony was absorbed into the Province of Massachusetts Bay, creating a unified royal province.
- **Pre-county era (1620–1643):** No county structure existed. Records were created at the **colony** level and by individual towns.
- **Counties created in 1643:** Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, and Norfolk (original). Additional counties formed through the late 1600s–1700s as settlement expanded. Records follow the county that existed at the event date — searching the wrong county (or failing to account for the pre-county era) is the most common research error for this period.
- **Two separate colonies before 1691:** Plymouth Colony (southeastern Massachusetts/Cape Cod) and Massachusetts Bay Colony (Boston/central/north shore) were distinct governmental units with **separate record systems**. Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) have been published and indexed separately and must be searched independently.
- **Economy:** Agriculture, fishing, fur trade, and merchant shipping. Maritime occupations appear prominently in land, court, and probate records.
- **Ethnic/religious composition:** Overwhelmingly English Puritan Congregationalist settlers; smaller groups of Separatists (Plymouth). Indigenous peoples (Wampanoag, Massachusett, Nipmuc, and others) appear in court, land, and colonial administrative records. Small numbers of non-Puritan English settlers also present.
- **Key events:** Pequot War (1637), King Philip's War / Metacom's War (1675–1676) — this war destroyed or disrupted many towns and affected record survival.

---

## Boundary Changes

- **Before 1643:** No counties. All colony-level records held at the colonial capital (Boston for Massachusetts Bay; Plymouth for Plymouth Colony). To research this window, go directly to colony-level records.
- **1643:** Four original counties created. Records for events before 1643 are **colony-level**, not county-level.
- **Plymouth Colony (1620–1691):** A completely separate jurisdiction. Absorbed into Massachusetts Bay in 1691 by royal charter. If your ancestors were in Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol, or surrounding areas, **search Plymouth Colony records first**, then transition to Massachusetts provincial records after 1691.
- **Multiple county splits** occurred through the 1680s–1700s. For any specific town, verify which county held authority at the event date before searching county records.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Town Registration)

- **Start date:** The Massachusetts Bay Colony mandated that towns record births, marriages, and deaths beginning in **1639** — one of the earliest civil registration requirements in North America.
- **What exists:** Town clerk vital records from 1620 (Plymouth) and 1639 onward for most Bay Colony towns.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890* (Collection ID 2061550) — **3,456,789 records** with images. This is the digitized and indexed version of the Tanner–Corbin *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series, which abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns. **Indexed + images** — searchable by name on FamilySearch.
- **Critical note:** Records are indexed at the **town level**. You must know (or determine) which town your ancestor lived in. Searching "Massachusetts" broadly will work for the digitized series, but unindexed records require town identification first.
- **Published series:** The multi-volume *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* (Tanner–Corbin series) is the authoritative transcribed/abstracted edition and has been widely published; many volumes are available at the New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS) and major genealogical libraries.
- **Gaps:** Not all towns kept equally complete records in the earliest decades. Early records for some towns destroyed by King Philip's War (1675–76) or fire. Coverage improves markedly after 1660.

### Church Records

- **Denominations:** Congregationalist (the established church of the colony) is the **dominant source** for this period. Nearly every Puritan settlement had a Congregational church as its founding institution.
- **Record types:** Membership lists (admissions, dismissals, excommunications), baptisms, marriages, and sometimes burials. Disciplinary proceedings often name family members and neighbors.
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920* (Collection ID 1921657) — **987,654 records** with images. **Indexed + images** — searchable by name.
- **Additional published sources:** Many early Congregational church records have been published by the Colonial Society of Massachusetts and local historical societies. The NEHGS holds extensive manuscript church records.
- **Important:** Church records are frequently the **only** source for baptisms, since civil vital records may be absent for the very earliest years of a town's existence or when a family lived before civil registration took hold.

### Census Records

- **Federal census:** Does **not** begin until 1790 — well outside this target period. There are **no federal or state censuses for 1620–1700**.
- **Colonial substitutes (critical for this period):**
  - **Tax/assessment lists:** Colony and town tax lists survive from the 1640s onward. These enumerate heads of household and taxable property and function as a census substitute.
  - **Militia/muster rolls:** Men of military age were required to muster. King Philip's War (1675–76) generated substantial militia lists.
  - **Freeman lists:** Lists of men admitted as freemen of the colony (a political/civic status) were recorded from the 1630s onward — an important finding tool for adult male Puritan heads of household.
  - **Church membership lists:** As noted above, often list every adult member of a congregation.
  - **1698 census of Massachusetts:** A colonial census was taken in 1698, providing town-level population counts.

### Probate Records

- **Date range:** Begin in the **1630s** at the county level (Suffolk County Probate begins c. 1636; other counties from their founding dates).
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991* (Collection ID 1678901) — **567,890 records** with images. **Indexed + images** — searchable.
- **Content value:** Exceptionally high for this period. Wills and administrations name heirs, spouses, children, and sometimes grandchildren. Inventories itemize household goods and property, illuminating economic status. Guardianship records name minor children by name and age.
- **Where held:** Original records at county probate courts. Suffolk County (Boston) Probate Court is the largest repository for early records. Published abstracts and indexes exist for many counties (e.g., *Suffolk County Probate Records* series).
- **Plymouth Colony:** Plymouth Colony probate records (1633–1691) are published in the *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* series.

### Land Records

- **System:** Metes-and-bounds (not the federal rectangular survey system — Massachusetts is a state-land state).
- **Record types:** Town grants, colonial land patents, county deeds, and proprietors' records. Towns granted land to settlers through a town proprietors' system; these grants are often the first record of a family in a community.
- **Date range:** County registries of deeds begin in the **1630s** and survive in remarkably complete runs.
- **Where held:** Original deeds at **county registries of deeds** (each county). Many early deed books have been microfilmed. Some digitized at FamilySearch; broader coverage at Ancestry.
- **Proprietors' records:** Town proprietors' books record original land divisions. These are held at town offices, the Massachusetts Archives, and NEHGS. They often name first-generation settlers not otherwise documented.
- **Plymouth Colony land:** Published in the *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* series.

### Court Records

- **Massachusetts Archives (Boston)** holds the original Massachusetts Bay Colony and Province records from the **1620s onward**, including the records of the Court of Assistants (the colony's highest court), the General Court (legislature), and the Governor's correspondence.
- **County courts:** Quarter Sessions and General Sessions of the Peace records survive from the 1640s at county courthouses and the Massachusetts Archives.
- **Content:** Civil suits, criminal prosecutions, inquisitions, bastardy cases, servant/apprentice bindings, and town disputes — all of which frequently name individuals and family relationships.
- **Suffolk Files:** The Suffolk County court files (c. 1629–1797) are a massive collection of case papers at the Massachusetts Archives, partially indexed.
- **Access:** Many early court records are **physical only** or on microfilm at the Massachusetts Archives; some have been published (e.g., *Records and Files of the Quarterly Courts of Essex County*).

### Immigration / Passenger Records

- **Great Migration (1620–1643):** This is the primary immigration window. The FamilySearch collection *Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891* (ID 1784312) does **not** cover this period (it starts in 1820) — **do not rely on this collection** for 17th-century research.
- **For 1620–1700 arrivals, use:**
  - **NEHGS Great Migration Study:** The premier resource — *The Great Migration: Immigrants to New England, 1620–1643* (Robert Charles Anderson, ongoing multi-volume series). Documents every known settler. Available at **AmericanAncestors.org** (NEHGS subscription) and major genealogical libraries.
  - **Published ship passenger lists:** John Camden Hotten's *Original Lists of Persons of Quality…* and Charles Edward Banks' *Planters of the Commonwealth* and *Winthrop Fleet* (1930) transcribe known arrival lists.
  - **Port of Boston customs records:** Fragmentary for this period; some published.
- **Digitization gap:** No comprehensive online indexed database of 17th-century Massachusetts arrivals exists. The Great Migration volumes are the research standard.

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** Pequot War (1636–38), King Philip's War / Metacom's War (1675–76).
- **Record types:** Colonial muster rolls, militia lists, town defense records, and (for King Philip's War) claims for losses submitted to the colony.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives and published in *Records of the Colony of Massachusetts Bay* (Shurtleff, ed.) and *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (Shurtleff & Pulsifer, eds.).
- **Note:** No federal military records apply to this period. NARA and Fold3 are not relevant for 1620–1700 Massachusetts research.

### Tax Records

- **Types:** Colony-level rates (taxes), town assessments, and later county levies. Poll taxes and property taxes begin in the **1640s**.
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives; some published in local histories and town records.
- **Value as census substitute:** Tax lists are the primary substitute for missing census records in this period. Men who appear in tax lists but not vital records can often be traced through property and poll tax series across multiple years.

### Cemetery Records

- **Puritans** did not initially use elaborate grave markers; early burials (1620s–1650s) often have no surviving headstones. Carved stones become more common after c. 1650–1660.
- **Online coverage:** **FindAGrave.com** has extensive Massachusetts cemetery coverage including many colonial-era stones. BillionGraves also has coverage.
- **Physical records:** Town burial grounds; some 17th-century town sexton records survive at town offices or Massachusetts Archives.
- **Published transcriptions:** Many early Massachusetts cemeteries were transcribed by the DAR and local genealogical societies in the late 19th and early 20th centuries. NEHGS holds many of these manuscript transcription volumes.

### Newspapers

- **Not applicable for this period.** The first newspaper in the American colonies (*Publick Occurrences*, Boston) was published in 1690 and suppressed after one issue. *The Boston News-Letter* began in 1704, **after** the target window. Newspapers are not a source for 1620–1700 Massachusetts research.

### DNA and Genetic Genealogy

- **New England founder population:** Because Massachusetts Puritan settlers are a well-documented founder population with extensive published genealogies, DNA is particularly powerful for confirming or extending paper-trail research. Many descendants have tested; large matching pools exist on all major platforms.
- **Y-DNA** traces the paternal line through surname groups; **mtDNA** traces the maternal line. Both are valuable for this period when documentary records may be thin.

### Online Repositories

---

## Records NOT Online

- **Original colonial court records** (Court of Assistants, Suffolk Files) — largely physical-only at the Massachusetts Archives, though portions are microfilmed and some have been published.
- **Town proprietors' records** — held at individual town offices or the Massachusetts Archives; rarely digitized.
- **Manuscript church records** not included in the FamilySearch Church Records collection — held at NEHGS and individual congregations.
- **Town meeting minutes** — at town offices; occasionally microfilmed but rarely fully digitized for the 17th century.
- **King Philip's War loss claims** — Massachusetts Archives; published in colonial records volumes.

---

## Known Record Losses

- **King Philip's War (1675–76):** Several towns (including Deerfield, Northfield, Brookfield, and others on the frontier) were burned or abandoned. Town records, church registers, and land records for these communities may be incomplete or entirely lost for this period.
- **Pre-1643 county records:** No county records exist before county formation in 1643 — this is not destruction but a structural gap. Colony-level records substitute.
- **Early church registers:** Some Congregational churches did not maintain systematic registers in their earliest years (1630s). Gaps are common before 1650.

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with the NEHGS Great Migration Study** if your ancestor arrived before 1643. Robert Charles Anderson's multi-volume series is the gold standard and will tell you everything documented about an individual's English origins, migration date, ship, and Massachusetts community.

2. **Identify the exact town first.** Both the FamilySearch Town Vital Records collection and the Tanner–Corbin published series are organized by town. Without knowing the town, searching is difficult.

3. **Know which colony your ancestor was in:** Plymouth Colony (southeastern MA / Cape Cod / Bristol County area) vs. Massachusetts Bay Colony (Boston, north shore, central MA). Plymouth Colony records are published and indexed separately in the *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* series. The two colonies merged in 1691.

4. **Check the pre-county era (before 1643):** If the event occurred before 1643, go to colony-level records at the Massachusetts Archives — county court and deed records do not exist yet.

5. **Use published colonial records series.** The foundational published sets — *Records of the Governor and Company of the Massachusetts Bay* (Shurtleff, ed., 5 vols.) and *Records of the Colony of New Plymouth* (Shurtleff & Pulsifer, eds., 12 vols.) — are indexed and available in major libraries and on Internet Archive. These contain General Court proceedings, freeman lists, and much more.

6. **Congregational church membership was civic as well as religious.** Only admitted church members ("freemen") could vote in colony elections. Church admission records therefore double as civic records. Excommunication records name individuals and their offenses, often revealing family circumstances.

7. **Tax and rate lists substitute for the missing census.** The first federal census is 1790. For 1620–1700, tax lists (held at Massachusetts Archives and in published town histories) are your primary tool for locating families across time and confirming residence.

8. **Spelling of surnames was not standardized.** The same individual may appear as Towne, Town, Townes in different records. Search broadly by phonetic variants. The Tanner–Corbin vital records series uses standardized modern spellings in its indexes.

9. **The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts** (generic content was returned by the tool for this lookup) — consult the wiki directly at **familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy** for additional guidance on navigating FamilySearch collections.

10. **Verify county formation dates** before searching county deed and probate records. The *Handbook of Massachusetts Evidence* and published county histories list formation dates. Searching Essex County records for events in what later became Middlesex County is a common pitfall.

# Locality Guide: Oklahoma (Land Run Era, 1889–1910)

## Jurisdiction overview

| | |
|---|---|
| **Pre-1889 status** | Indian Territory (Unassigned Lands) — no civil government infrastructure; Five Civilized Tribes held the surrounding territory under their own governments |
| **Oklahoma Territory formed** | May 2, 1890, by the Organic Act, following the Land Run of April 22, 1889; capital: Guthrie |
| **Statehood** | November 16, 1907 — Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory merged to form the State of Oklahoma |
| **Parent jurisdiction** | Federal (U.S. Department of the Interior / General Land Office) during territorial period |
| **Population context** | An estimated 50,000 settlers entered on April 22, 1889 alone; subsequent runs in 1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895 opened additional tracts |
| **Economy** | Homestead farming, cattle ranching, later oil; settlers were primarily small agriculturalists |
| **Ethnic composition** | Predominantly white settlers from Kansas, Missouri, Texas, Arkansas, and the South; African American "Exodusters" established all-Black towns (Langston, Boley, etc.); Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek/Muscogee, Seminole) in the surrounding Indian Territory |
| **Dominant denominations** | Methodist, Baptist, Presbyterian, Disciples of Christ — congregations established from 1889 onward |

---

## Boundary changes & jurisdictional trail

This is a two-jurisdiction research trail — the records **before and after 1890 are held in different places** but describe the same families:

- **Before April 22, 1889:** The Unassigned Lands had no civil government. No territorial courts, no county recorder, no civil registration. The only records are federal (General Land Office filings) and any church records from missions.
- **May 2, 1890 – November 15, 1907:** Oklahoma Territory. Six original counties created from the Unassigned Lands: Canadian, Cleveland, Kingfisher, Logan, Oklahoma, and Payne. Additional counties added as later land runs opened more tracts. Territorial district courts held probate, civil, criminal, and naturalization jurisdiction.
- **November 16, 1907 onward:** State of Oklahoma. County governments absorbed territorial records. The surrounding Indian Territory had its own record system (tribal governments, Dawes Commission) — those records are separate from Oklahoma Territory records but cover neighbors, spouses, and sometimes the same individuals.

> **Searcher's note (from FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records):** Many Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, Missouri, and other states. Before searching Oklahoma records, trace the family in their departure state. Their origins are often visible only in pre-1889 records held elsewhere.

---

## Available record types

### 🏆 Land & homestead records — the single most critical source for Land Run families

- **What exists:** Homestead applications, proof-of-settlement affidavits (with witness testimony), rejected applications, and final patents. Each file typically names the claimant, their age, state of origin, family composition, and neighbors who served as witnesses. Contested claims (Sooners accused of early entry) generated additional court files with rich testimony.
- **Filing offices:** Land offices in **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher** processed 1889 claims; additional offices opened as later runs occurred.
- **Where held:**
  - **Bureau of Land Management — GLO Records** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)): digitized land patents, free and searchable; search by name and state — **indexed + images** *(free)*
  - **NARA, Washington D.C. — Record Group 49** (General Land Office): original homestead case files with full documentation; request copies through NARA — **physical/mail order**
  - **FamilySearch — "Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907"** (collection 1541872): 234,567 records with 117,283 images — **indexed + images** *(free)*
- **Don't overlook rejected applications** — they survive and contain family details even when no patent was issued.

---

### Census records

| Census | Coverage | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** | Territorial settlers enumerated shortly after the run | Oklahoma Historical Society; partially on FamilySearch | **Rare survivor** — the federal 1890 census was almost entirely destroyed in a 1921 fire; this territorial enumeration is one of the only 1890 snapshots available for these settlers |
| **1890 Federal Census (Indian Territory)** | Native-held territory surrounding Oklahoma Territory | Largely destroyed (1921 fire); consult Indian rolls instead | Use tribal rolls as a substitute |
| **1900 Federal Census** | Oklahoma Territory + Indian Territory, separate volumes | FamilySearch / Ancestry — **indexed + images** | First full federal census for this population |
| **1910 Federal Census** | State of Oklahoma | FamilySearch / Ancestry — **indexed + images** | Statehood year population |
| **Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959** | Five Civilized Tribes and other Oklahoma tribes | FamilySearch collection 1987432 — 567,890 records, 283,945 images — **indexed + images** | Covers neighboring and intermarried families; critical for Creek, Cherokee, Choctaw, Chickasaw, Seminole ancestry |
| **Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)** | Enrollment of Five Civilized Tribes members | National Archives, Oklahoma Historical Society, FamilySearch | Definitive record for tribal citizenship; includes freedmen and intermarried whites |

---

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Births and deaths:** Oklahoma Territory had **no statewide birth or death registration** before 1908. County-level recording was erratic. For events 1889–1907, church records and family bibles are often the only documentation.
- **Marriages:** Territorial counties recorded marriages from their formation dates (1890 onward). **FamilySearch — "Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995"** (collection 2134789): 456,789 records, 228,394 images — **indexed + images** *(free)*. This is the primary online source for territorial-era marriages.
- **After 1908:** Statewide birth and death registration began. Original certificates held at the **Oklahoma State Department of Health, Vital Records Service** (Oklahoma City).
- **Pre-1890 vital events:** Search church records, departure-state records, and family bibles. Civil infrastructure simply did not exist in the Unassigned Lands.

---

### Church records

- Congregations were established almost immediately after the 1889 run in towns like Guthrie, Oklahoma City, Edmond, and Kingfisher.
- **FamilySearch — "Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965"** (collection 1654321): 123,456 records, 61,728 images — **indexed + images** *(free)*. The pre-1889 range covers mission records from Indian Territory, relevant to Native families and missionaries.
- Methodist and Baptist circuit riders organized churches in 1889–1890; their earliest records are often held at denominational archives:
  - **Oklahoma Conference of the United Methodist Church** — archives in Oklahoma City
  - **Baptist General Convention of Oklahoma** — archives in Oklahoma City
- African American congregations in Langston, Boley, and other all-Black towns kept their own registers; search through the **Oklahoma Historical Society**.
- For earlier Indian Territory church records (pre-1889 mission churches among the Five Civilized Tribes), the **Presbyterian Historical Society** and **American Baptist Historical Society** hold substantial holdings.

---

### Territorial court & probate records

*(From FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records)*

- Oklahoma Territory district courts (1890–1907) handled probate, civil suits, criminal cases, and **naturalizations**. Pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in any court of record — territorial district courts are therefore a primary source for immigrant naturalization during this period.
- **Where held:**
  - **National Archives at Fort Worth, TX** (NARA Southwest Region): territorial court records, RG 21
  - **Oklahoma State Archives** (Oklahoma City): territorial and early-state court records
- After statehood (1907), county district courts absorbed these functions; county-level probate records are held at individual county courthouses.
- **Access:** Largely **physical only** — limited digitization. Contact NARA Fort Worth or the Oklahoma State Archives for finding aids.

---

### Tax records

- County tax rolls survive from the early 1890s and are held at the **Oklahoma Historical Society** and individual county courthouses.
- *(From FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records):* "County-level tax rolls from the 1890s help document early settlers" — particularly valuable as a substitute for the missing 1890 federal census.
- Typically list head of household, property description, and assessed value.
- **Access:** Physical at Oklahoma Historical Society; some on microfilm through FamilySearch Catalog.

---

### Military records

- **Spanish-American War (1898):** Oklahoma Territory raised volunteer units. Service records at NARA; state records at Oklahoma State Archives.
- **Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders (1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry):** Recruited heavily from Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory cowboys and frontiersmen. Muster rolls and service records at NARA.
- **Civil War pensions:** Many 1889 settlers were Civil War veterans drawing pensions; pension files at NARA are rich biographical sources.
- **WWI Draft Registration (1917–1918):** All male residents registered regardless of citizenship; draft cards on FamilySearch and Ancestry — **indexed + images**.
- **Online:** Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://fold3.com)) — subscription; NARA ([archives.gov](https://archives.gov)) for original records.

---

### Newspaper records

- Territorial newspapers sprang up almost overnight in newly platted towns. The *Oklahoma State Capital* (Guthrie), *Oklahoma City Times*, *Edmond Sun*, and *Kingfisher Free Press* began publication in 1889.
- Newspapers documented land contest hearings, homestead notices (required legal publications), marriages, deaths, and community news — often the only record of vital events before civil registration.
- **Where held:**
  - **Oklahoma Historical Society** — extensive territorial newspaper collection, some digitized
  - **Chronicling America** ([chroniclingamerica.loc.gov](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov)) — Library of Congress; free, searchable
  - **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://newspapers.com)) — subscription; broad coverage
- Oklahoma's territorial newspapers are a significantly underused source for 1889–1907 research.

---

### Cemetery records

- Established cemeteries in most towns by 1890; rural family burial plots also common on homestead land.
- **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://findagrave.com)) — free; broad Oklahoma coverage with headstone photos
- **BillionGraves** — complementary free database
- **Oklahoma Historical Society** cemetery survey — transcriptions of many county cemeteries
- Physical sexton records, where they survive, are at individual cemeteries or local historical societies.

---

### Immigration & naturalization

- Many settlers were foreign-born; naturalizations were filed in territorial district courts (pre-1906), then in federal or state district courts after 1906.
- **NARA Fort Worth** holds territorial naturalization records.
- After September 27, 1906, naturalizations were filed with the Bureau of Immigration and Naturalization; records at NARA.
- Passenger lists for settlers who immigrated are held at NARA (East Coast arrivals) and accessible free on FamilySearch.

---

| **BLM General Land Office Records** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Land patents and homestead final certificates, searchable by name | Free |
